#2859. Trump says ‘we don’t need a deal with Iran’

The U.S. should no longer seek a deal with Iran, President Donald Trump said Thursday as he directed Vice President JD Vance to instead focus his attention on corruption and crime in Democratic cities and states.

"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

"We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" Trump wrote, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, a key choke point in the ongoing U.S.-Iran war.

The announcement came just over a week after Republicans suffered huge losses in the midterm election. Vance and other Republicans have pinned those losses on the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel started in late February.

In the weeks leading up to Election Day, Trump repeatedly suggested the U.S. could resume launching military strikes, which have largely subsided as a tense stalemate has taken hold in the region.

The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday reported that Vance, who has led diplomatic efforts with Iran in prior months, was considering face-to-face talks with a top Iranian security official.

Stock futures declined following Trump's post.

The unpopular Iran war, which Trump and others in his administration said would be won in a matter of weeks, is now in its ninth month with no clear end in sight. The conflict has driven up global energy prices, creating a ripple effect through the economy and exacerbating concerns about inflation and affordability that were paramount to voters in the midterms.

Corruption emerged as another top issue that broke in Democrats' favor in the election. Trump's post Thursday morning attempts to flip the script, blaming Democratic-run areas for allowing corruption and crime to proliferate.

"I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.," Trump wrote.

"The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters. Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month," the president wrote. "Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity."

"CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership's blood!" he added.

#2858. IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap: What it means for your money

The IRS has announced new retirement account contribution limits for 2027.

In its release on Thursday, the agency increased the 401(k) employee deferral limit to $25,500 next year, up from $24,500 in 2026. The change applies to 401(k)s, 403(b)s and most 457 plans, along with the federal Thrift Savings Plan.

The IRS also unveiled 2027 catch-up contribution limits for savers age 50 and older, new individual retirement account savings limits and higher income thresholds for Roth IRA contributions.

Starting in 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution limit will rise to $8,500 for savers 50 and older, up from $8,000 in 2026. But investors aged 60 to 63 can instead save an extra $11,750, based on changes enacted via Secure 2.0. That figure is up $500 from 2026.

Both amounts are in addition to the $25,500 deferral limit for 2027.

The 2027 IRA contribution limit is $7,500, unchanged from 2026, the IRS announced. IRA catch-up contributions for investors age 50 and older will be $1,100, the same as 2026.

The announcement comes one week after the agency released dozens of other inflation adjustments for 2027, including federal income tax brackets, higher capital gains brackets, estate and gift tax exemptions and provisions impacting families, among others.

In 2025, only 14% of participants maxed out their 401(k)s, according to Vanguard's 2026 How America Saves report, which was based on data from more than 1,300 qualified plans and nearly 5 million participants. The average combined savings rate, including employer deposits, was an estimated 12.1%, according to the same report.

"Before worrying about contribution limits, make sure you're capturing your full employer match," said Sean Michael Pearson, a certified financial planner with Ameriprise Financial Services in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania.

During the second quarter of 2026, about 19% of employees weren't deferring enough to 401(k)s to receive their company's full matching contribution, according to a Fidelity analysis of 27,300 corporate plans and nearly 26 million participants.

Vanguard suggests saving 12% to 15% of your pay per year, including employer contributions, depending on your income. But only one-quarter of 401(k) participants deferred more than 10% of earnings in 2025, according to Vanguard's report.

If you plan to max out your 401(k) for 2027, you should change your savings rate in December so it's active by your first January paycheck, experts say. The update could take one or two pay periods to go into effect.

The "most important habit" is consistently increasing your 401(k) savings rate over time, according to Pearson.

For example, if you bump 401(k) contributions by 1% every year, "you may barely notice the difference in your paycheck, but the long-term impact can be substantial," he said.

In 2025, about 27% of 401(k) plans automatically increased employee deferrals over time, known as "auto-escalation," according to the Plan Sponsor Council of America's yearly survey of 401(k)s. The nonprofit trade organization's survey included 753 plans.

The vast majority of plans with auto-escalation, 69%, boosted deferrals by 1% per year, the Plan Sponsor Council of America found.

#2857. Widespread Microsoft outage takes down Outlook and other 365 services

Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday that impacted thousands of users across regions, according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.com.

The outage began shortly before 1 p.m. and impacted Microsoft 365 services, Outlook and Teams. At the time, about 130,000 users reported issues with Outlook.

Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site.

"We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online," a Microsoft spokesperson wrote in a statement to CNBC. "We appreciate our customers' patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible."

Microsoft shared updates on the outage from its Microsoft 365 Status account on social media platform X.

Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."

At 4 p.m., Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.

"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."

Microsoft initially said infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions" was responsible for the connectivity problems.

The company later determined that the elevated load was caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure" and that some servers were failing automated health checks.

"We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service," Microsoft wrote.

#2856. Can Warriors survive without Stephen Curry with tough stretch ahead?

On Thursday, the Golden State Warriors announced that star guard Steph Curry was diagnosed with an oblique abdominal tear and will be shelved for at least the next two weeks. The 38-year-old suffered the injury midway through the first quarter of Wednesday's 115-108 loss to the Houston Rockets.

For a team and organization that has orbited around Curry's generational gravity for nearly two decades, the loss is significant. Prior to Wednesday's loss (Curry played just five minutes), he had been averaging near-identical production to his 2016 MVP season.

The 18-year veteran has been able to shoulder a seismic load — due to the absence of Jimmy Butler and Kristaps Porziņģis' abrupt decision to step away from basketball citing health reasons — handling the ball more than ever and converting shots at the most efficient rate, all while minimizing turnovers. Curry has been the driving force for the 8-4 Warriors, who have won eight of their past nine games, which is nothing short of a testament to his greatness amid a loaded Western Conference and a team that, on paper, pales in comparison to its peers.

The Warriors will be without Stephen Curry for at least two weeks.

The Warriors' next seven games offer quite the challenge. In the coming fortnight, Golden State will face San Antonio, Dallas, Memphis, Boston and Portland, which have all won more than 60% of their games to date. But amid those upcoming hurdles, there's a strong belief within the locker room that the roster as-is can withstand Curry's absence in the short term.

"The spirit of this team is better," forward Draymond Green said to reporters following the game. "We're more certain of who we are, what makes us a good team. That puts us in a better position to be successful without him as opposed to where we were last year."

Green's assessment checks out. In 317 non-Curry minutes, the Warriors have been able to outscore teams by 14 points, according to PBP Stats, a substantial improvement from last season (Golden State lost those minutes by a whopping 135 points). The improvement of fourth-year guard Brandin Podziemski, who will now come into focus as the team's biggest perimeter threat, will be tested in the interim. Albeit in a much-smaller role alongside Curry, Podziemski has been able to clean up his shot profile and ball security, two areas of focus for him since he was drafted in 2023. This season, Podz has taken on a much larger playmaking role when Curry is off the floor and is able to draw more fouls — in addition to excelling in transition and off-ball activity.

There's also the presence of rookie Yaxel Lendeborg, a Swiss Army knife of a combo forward that is equal parts thrilling and chaotic, who has taken on enough responsibility early on and converted his chances at veteran-level clips, currently in the 87th percentile of rim success and 79th in perimeter success, according to Cleaning the Glass. The first-year phenom is the team's second-leading scorer, averaging 21.7 points per game.

If the Warriors are to survive these next two weeks, they'll need to further emphasize their unselfish identity. Without Curry's gravity, ball movement becomes even more of a premium. They're second in passes made, third in assists and first in secondary assists because of a starting lineup that possesses five players who can create with the ball in their hands to varying degrees (Lendeborg, Podziemski, Al Horford, Draymond Green and the insertion of De'Anthony Melton, who likely picks up the minutes void and is a capable creator on his own).

(Melton's presence also juices the Warriors' penchant for forcing turnovers. They're surprisingly ninth in half-court defensive efficiency, fifth in opponent turnover rate and are good at turning mistakes into points, eighth-best at the time of this writing.)

The most important factor, however, during this period of uncertainty, is the leadership structure between Green and Kerr. Those two and Curry have been the lone constants over the years, and with Curry gone, Green and Kerr should be the consistent go-tos for guidance and morale.

They share a deep understanding and longevity that transcend most partnerships in sports. And they aren't new to uncomfortable situations — whether it's internal drama, injuries, or the growing pains that come with two-timeline situations.

"I was thrilled that the guys stayed together," Kerr said after Wednesday's game. "It's a great group to coach. I really love this team and I'm excited about what's ahead."

Make no mistake, Curry's absence, even if it's for two weeks, will be felt every time this team steps on the floor. But the energy about this new group, despite the lack of outside expectations, is tangible and might just be enough to hold down the fort until 30 is ready to go again.

#2854. As Nvidia reels from Huang's affairs, who stands to gain?

Nvidia's leadership crisis is creating an opening for its biggest rivals as well as partners, as investors bet that Jensen Huang's departure could loosen the AI chip giant's grip on an industry it has long dominated.

From AMD to Broadcom and even partner TSMC, chipmakers are emerging as potential beneficiaries of the upheaval, with market watchers pointing to a possible redistribution of manufacturing capacity and a narrowing of Nvidia's technological lead.

"What you're seeing in markets now is a bit of a rotation into other advanced chip design companies, on the assumption that this will enable other companies effectively to catch up," said Mark Franklin, head of multi-asset solutions for Asia at Manulife Investment Management.

That shift comes as Nvidia grapples with the fallout from Huang's resignation, following revelations about his multiple affairs including with a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy.

Huang's departure could give competitors an opportunity to close the gap as Nvidia navigates leadership uncertainty, Franklin highlighted, adding that the rotation was already helping fuel positive momentum in other semiconductor stocks.

Farzin Azam, managing director of equities trading at Mizuho Americas, said the shift was evident on trading desks, with investors moving toward chipmakers less exposed to Nvidia's management turmoil.

"Names such as TSMC, names such as Broadcom, names such as Advanced Micro will come as winners of this because they don't have this overhang of a management disruption," Azam told CNBC.

Nvidia shares have plunged 11% so far this week, while rivals AMD and Broadcom have gained 30% and 24%, respectively.

TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's most advanced processors, has also rallied 11% over the same period, as it stands to benefit, irrespective of which chip designer gains or loses. A rotation away from AI names perceived as risky also positions TSMC as a relatively safer play for those bullish on the overall theme.

The rotation away from Nvidia has also extended into less speculative corners of the semiconductor industry, including analog chipmakers such as Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and Infineon, as investors adopt a more defensive stance, he said.

Texas Instruments has climbed about 13% this week, while Analog Devices and Germany's Infineon have advanced 12% and 14%, respectively.

Beyond the immediate market reaction, Huang's exit could fundamentally reshape competition across the AI supply chain, according to Dylan Patel, chief executive at semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis.

Patel said Huang had personally cultivated relationships with manufacturers and component suppliers, helping Nvidia secure scarce production capacity ahead of rivals.

That advantage could now come under pressure as companies including Google and Amazon strive to expand AI chip production.

The two hyperscalers were already gaining ground in securing supply-chain capacity relative to Nvidia, Patel said, and could accelerate those efforts without Huang's influence over suppliers.

"If Nvidia can't muster the supply chain, then technology is the only competitive advantage. And without Jensen, can they maintain technology advantages? Given they're only a year ahead of their biggest competitors, it's not like the gap is massive," Patel said.

The challenge is particularly acute as hyperscalers increasingly develop proprietary AI chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, while AMD and other semiconductor companies race to capture a larger slice of the market.

Yet the upheaval doesn't necessarily signal an end to the broader AI investment boom.

Franklin noted that major technology companies are projecting higher AI spending in 2027, with further increases possible in 2028, signaling the investment cycle remains structurally intact even as investors reassess which companies stand to benefit.

The bigger question is whether growing competition and the proliferation of open-source technologies eventually commoditize AI capabilities, putting pressure on chip prices and investment returns, he said.

For Nvidia, the immediate outlook may depend less on its earnings than on whether its next leadership team can reassure investors.

Azam said the stock appeared inexpensive relative to its earnings growth prospects, but warned that ongoing investigations and management uncertainty could limit any sustained recovery.

He expects Nvidia's earnings due Nov. 17 to remain strong, with investors likely to focus more closely on management's plans for navigating the crisis.

The result could be a reshuffling of winners within the semiconductor industry, with Franklin saying that investors were becoming more comfortable staying invested while rotating and diversifying their portfolios, instead of abandoning the market altogether.

#2853. Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor

Alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, at the same time that she was in business with Nvidia and also reportedly having a romantic affair with its ousted CEO Jensen Huang.

The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei was first discovered by analysts at private intelligence firm Tesari. The firm exclusively shared its findings with CNBC. Tesari, which uses artificial intelligence to collect evidence and specializes in national security investigations around the world, provides intelligence research to private companies and the U.S. government.

This previously unreported entanglement may raise questions about Alice Huang's intent and conduct in her relationship with the CEO and whether Jensen Huang knew his romantic partner was closely connected with his competition. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an affair, though the precise timing of his relationship with Alice Huang is unknown.

The mysterious saga of Alice Huang involves a tangle of interlocking corporations and transactions that show her connection to entities that ultimately provided computing power to Huawei in China.

Huawei is known as a Chinese government "state champion" in the technology and telecommunications sectors, meaning it receives enormous financial support from the government in Beijing so it can lower prices and undercut global competitors. It is considered a key part of the Chinese government's push for global technical dominance and is closely linked to the Chinese Communist Party.

Businesses connected to Alice Huang were linked with supplying Nvidia computing power to Huawei, according to documents reviewed by CNBC, around the same time she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together, in December 2023.

In 2024, Nvidia said Huawei was a top competitor, specifically in artificial intelligence chips including graphics processing units, central processing units and networking chips.

"This activity, which surfaced through our analysis of Alice's network, warrants a national security and [technology] counterproliferation investigation," said Brian Andersen, Tesari's vice president for national security applications and a former supervisory special agent with Homeland Security Investigations.

If the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry Security and Homeland Security Investigations found evidence that anyone transferred "controlled equipment" to Huawei without authorization, potential charges might include export-control violations, conspiracy and smuggling, Andersen said.

The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei is so convoluted that analysts at Tesari told CNBC that based on their previous investigative experience, they suspect it was designed to deliberately obscure the relationship.

Nvidia and Huawei did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. Jensen Huang did not respond to a voicemail left on a mobile phone. Alice Huang could not be reached.

According to Chinese corporate records and media reports compiled by Tesari and provided to CNBC, Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le and who according to documents at the time was based in Hong Kong, in 2019 sold a cloud business she owned called Osmanthus to a Chinese gaming company called 7Road. A subsidiary of 7Road, which was based in Singapore, was spun off as "Megaspeed" in 2023. Megaspeed would go on to become a key Nvidia customer, helping facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, The Information reported Tuesday.

As early as 2016, Alice Huang had also become a co-owner of a financial firm known as Shanghai Hexi, which heavily invests in tech and data centers. In 2021, Hexi in turn acquired 27 percent of a company called Shanghai Century Longteng, a data center developer, which Hexi held until 2024. That firm owned a controlling 50.1 percent stake in a data center facility called Shenzhen Yifeng Technology Co. Ltd. in mainland China.

The key customer of that data center was Huawei Cloud, the Shenzhen, China-based subsidiary of Huawei Technologies.

In addition, Alice Huang's firm Hexi guaranteed the loans required to finance the Shenzhen data center, which did business with Huawei.

Hexi did not immediately respond to a message via its LinkedIn page sent outside of normal business hours.

CNBC translated corporate records and Chinese news articles in Mandarin that Tesari provided.

It's not clear if the Shenzhen data center was able to acquire Nvidia GPUs, but its majority owner began purchasing the chips in 2023. That company is known as Zhejiang Century Huatong Group and is a business partner of Alice Huang's Hexi through their joint ownership of Century Longteng.

That made Alice Huang a part owner of a data center providing computing power to Huawei. And that was happening at around the same time the first known sightings of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang in public together.

And that raises the question of why Huawei, which has access to Chinese-made chips, would need to rent computing power from an outside entity.

Hexi exited its stake in the data center development company in 2024, but individuals within Alice Huang's network are still connected to the Shenzhen data center. Her husband Kang Wei is a longtime business associate who founded Hexi, where Alice Huang previously held an executive role. In 2022, Kang became an executive of Century Longteng, which owns the controlling stake in the Shenzhen data center, and he also attended the company's signing of the Huawei agreement.

#2851. Ravens' Mark Andrews learned to deal with adversity at age 9 following Type 1 diabetes diagnosis

Being diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes as a kid prepared Baltimore Ravens tight end Mark Andrews for adversity in the NFL.

Andrews has made three Pro Bowls, been an All-Pro and has played on six playoff teams in his first eight seasons. He dropped a pass on a 2-point conversion that would've tied the game in his last playoff game, a 27-25 loss to Buffalo in the AFC divisional round on Jan. 19, 2025.

"I've been ready for this like my whole life," Andrews said on the AP's "Football Unfiltered" podcast. "Being diagnosed Type 1 diabetes at the age of 9, I've been able to kind of mature at an early age and do things that other kids didn't have to do or think about and live my life in a certain way that is constant 24-7 kind of surveillance and so I'm always looking kind of inward and I've always been able to do that and I don't look outward to whatever maybe like media or outside sources to get gratification.

"For me, just being able to stay focused and believe in the people around me, believe in the work that I put in, all kind of goes back to being really diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes at a young age and trying to prove people wrong and that I can do anything I want in life. And no matter what life kind of hands you, you should keep on going, you keep on working hard and good things will happen."

Andrews suffered a near-fatal severe hypoglycemic episode while taking a nap in his dorm room during his freshman year at Oklahoma in September 2014. After that incident, he began wearing a Dexcom device that tracks his glucose levels.

"I wear a Dexcom G7 and it's incredible for me as an athlete just being able to have real-time blood glucose results and getting those blood sugar numbers in real time really helps you manage your diabetes," he said.

Andrews and the Ravens (4-5) are going through a rough stretch right now. The team has lost four straight games and three-time All-Pro quarterback Lamar Jackson is on injured reserve because of a thumb injury.

Baltimore was down to third-string quarterback Joe Fagnano after backup Tyler Huntley suffered a season-ending toe injury so veteran Jacoby Brissett was acquired from Arizona. Brissett will start Monday night against the winless Los Angeles Chargers (0-8).

It's been a tough first half for first-year coach Jesse Minter, who replaced John Harbaugh and took over a team that entered the season among the Super Bowl favorites.

"He's been great," Andrews said of Minter. "Just his messaging to the team, his confidence, all these types of things, he's just so steady and it's not easy. I think that if we just stay true to ourselves, we still have so many great players and guys that still want it so bad. #2850. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

#2849. Joel Embiid scores 20 in 76ers' win over Raptors after knee injury scare; LeBron James sat out for back management

After being listed as questionable up until game time, Joel Embiid scored 20 points in the Philadelphia 76ers' 123-112 win over the Toronto Raptors on Thursday.

Embiid also avoided what initially appeared to be a knee injury early in the first quarter when Ja'Kobe Walter ran into him trying to avoid a screen. Walter's right knee collided with Embiid's right knee, sending the center to the floor. Embiid pointed to his knee as trainers came out to check him, causing fears that he may have been seriously hurt.

However, Embiid re-entered the game three minutes later and scored his first basket with under two minutes remaining in the first quarter.

Up until a half-hour before tip-off, Embiid was listed on the injury report as questionable with "right foot plantar fascia injury management." That had also sidelined him for two of the Sixers' game in the early season.

"I have no idea," Embiid said when asked by ESPN's Kris Rhim during shootaround if he was playing versus the Raptors. "We'll see what they have to say and then we'll go from there."

Tyrese Maxey scored 27 to lead the Sixers, also dishing out 8 assists. Jaylen Brown added 18 with 6 rebounds, Anfernee Simons contributed 17 points (hitting 5-of-6 3-pointers) off the bench and VJ Edgecombe finished with 15 points, 8 board, 8 assists and 3 steals. Philadelphia improved its record to 9-3, 5-2 at home.

For the Raptors, RJ Barrett led all scorers with 31 points (shooting 4-for-7 on 3s) in addition to 14 rebounds and 5 assists. Immanuel Quickley added 26 points, 4 rebounds and 6 assists. Collin Murray-Boyles scored 14 points with 4 assists and 5 blocks. Toronto dropped to 5-7 (3-4 on the road) with the defeat.

While Embiid played, LeBron James sat out his third game of the early 2026-27 season on Thursday. James was listed on the Sixers' injury report as out with "low back/sciatica management," which had been the reason he's sat two of Philadelphia's previous 12 games this season.

The 41-year-old was listed as questionable until participating in Thursday's shootaround. He was then downgraded.

Thursday's game was not part of a back-to-back for the 76ers, so that was not a consideration in sitting James and possibly resting Embiid. Philadelphia last played on Tuesday, losing 123-101 to the Boston Celtics in the hyped first meeting between former teammates Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum.

However, the Sixers do play back-to-back games on Sunday and Monday, hosting the Indiana Pacers then visiting the Brooklyn Nets.

So far this season, James is averaging 15.1 points, 7.2 rebounds and 6.5 assists on 43% shooting from the floor. Embiid is scoring 17.7 points per game with 9.3 rebounds and 3.8 assists. He is also shooting 37%, while making only 4 of 33 (12%) 3-point attempts.

#2848. Failed Daiyan Henley trade exposes a flaw in the NFL's trade deadline

The trade deadline is the trade deadline. Except when it’s not the trade deadline.

The strange situation involving the failed trade of Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley to the Broncos reveals a major flaw in the NFL’s deadline-day machinery.

Adam Schefter of ESPN has provided the details (which we have confirmed to be accurate) in the most nonchalant, innocuous terms possible: “It is not uncommon for one team to have some medical concerns about a player while another does not. In this case, Denver had concerns about Henley following his physical. Even then, the Broncos still wanted Henley with Denver and LA discussing revised trade alternatives throughout the day, taking into account those concerns. In the end, no agreement was reached. The deal was off.”

Here’s what it means. The Chargers and Broncos struck a deal for Henley and independently communicated the terms to the NFL before the trade deadline of 4:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10. Like all trades, the Henley deal was subject to the player passing a physical.

The Broncos discovered an issue with Henley’s knee. It has, we’re told, arthritis. (As one source with neither the Chargers nor the Broncos told PFT, most if not all starting linebackers in the NFL have some degree of arthritis in their knees.)

The NFL allows trade terms to be revised after the deadline, to an extent. Per a league spokesperson: “We would permit them to change the pick compensation. They would not be able to add a player or trade a different player.”

Instead of concluding that the physical had been failed and canceling the deal (like the Ravens did with the trade for Raiders defensive end Maxx Crosby in March), the Broncos were willing to proceed with revised terms. In other words, for something less than a fourth-round pick in 2027 and a fifth-round pick in 2028, they’d still do the deal.

That’s not how it should work after the deadline. The window has closed. The deals are done, or they’re not. After 4:00 p.m. ET on November 10, the only question left to answer is whether the player passes or fails the physical.

As one source explained it, deadline-day deals have gone through in the past with terms that were revised after the deadline.

Based on Schefter’s reporting, that’s what happened here. The Broncos had “medical concerns,” but not enough to reject the player. The Broncos and Chargers discussed “revised trade alternatives” on Wednesday — the day after the window for doing trades ended.

The Chargers could have taken less in order to get the deal done. They chose not to do so. The fact that the rules allow trade terms to be renegotiated after the deadline opened the door for the Broncos to squeeze the Chargers.

The situation creates an opportunity for shenanigans. If, for example, Team A is preparing to trade a player to Team B at the deadline for a fourth-round pick and a sixth-round pick, Team C can swoop in and offer a fourth-round pick and a fifth-round pick. Then, when the physical is performed after the deadline, Team C can say, “Well, we have medical concerns. If we don’t agree to reduce the package to a fourth-round pick and a sixth-round pick, we’re going to fail the player on his physical.”

That’s not to say the Broncos did it deliberately. Obviously, however, they remained interested in Henley (who has started all eight games this year and has participated in 89 percent of the snaps) at something less than the agreed terms.

The point is that this little-known ability to extend the trading period by giving the acquiring team the ability to use the physical to leverage better terms shouldn’t exist. When a deal is done at the deadline, the trade should either go through for the agreed terms or it shouldn’t.

It opens the door to gamesmanship. The team that has traded the player has no alternatives. It can’t trade the player to someone else. It either has to accept reduced terms or try to put the toothpaste back in the tube.

The Vikings, for example, could have tried to do that to the Raiders regarding quarterback Kirk Cousins. “Well, we found something in Kirk’s leg that we don’t like. We’re not comfortable giving up a third-round pick. How about a fifth-round pick instead?”

What would the Raiders have done at that point? They’d already turned the page to Fernando Mendoza, and they spent Tuesday and Wednesday getting him ready to play.

The rule needs to change. The ability to revisit trade terms after the deadline has passed should be eliminated. Either the deal gets done as negotiated, or it doesn’t.

Hovering over all of this is the subjectivity that can result in a team failing a player on a physical if it wants that outcome. It’s an easy way out for a team that has buyer’s remorse. (The Bengals, for example, could have determined that Eagles defensive end Arnold Ebiketie failed his physical, if the Bengals hadn’t realized until after the trade terms were finalized that the Bengals would lose a 2027 third-round compensatory pick if the trade became official.)

At some point, it makes sense for the physicals not to be conducted by team doctors but by an independent, unaffiliated physician. But that’s for another day. For now, the immediate problem that needs to be solved is the ability of teams to renegotiate trade terms after the trade deadline.

No one benefits from that, and unscrupulous teams could use it to their advantage.

#2843. Why the Colorado Buffaloes Now Have Better Odds to Make the College Football Playoff —in 2027

The Colorado Buffaloes have had a season to remember—for all the things not to do next season.

Despite being on the cusp of back-to-back losing seasons, there could be light at the end of the tunnel. With the official approval of the 24-team expansion of the College Football Playoff, Deion Sanders and the Buffs could have a chance to make their first-ever appearance next year.

Every Power 4 school will try for one of 19 automatic bids with a chance to host a playoff game on their campus. Here's the catch to it all. If Sanders and his staff can duplicate the success from the 2024 season, they'll likely be Playoff bound. However, the biggest elephant in the room is, will Coach Prime be in Boulder long enough to make the postseason?

The margin for error has greatly increased, and with the removal of conference championship games, every team has a fair shot.

Colorado hoped for a culture change with Sanders, but instead got a repeat of history with only one winning season in his tenure thus far. There's always room for improvement. The new CFP format may have just bought the Hall of Fame cornerback another year. The regular season games will no longer have must-win stakes. Because now a three or four-loss team can punch their ticket for a shot at a national championship. A team like Colorado should be licking its chops at an opportunity to be part of the final 24 teams.

If they were to finish 9-3, it would almost guarantee them a playoff berth. However, they wouldn't be the only unlikely team sniffing glory. The biggest concern is whether Coach Prime can lead his team to another 9-win season without Heisman winner Travis Hunter and his sons, Shedeur and Shilo. It has yet to be done and doesn't look like it will happen in the foreseeable future. Outside of Prime's expensive buyout to the tune of $26 million, the Buffs are keeping him for the 'what if' factor.

What if he can achieve another 9-4 season without his sons and one of the best players in college football history?

For now, though, Colorado will need to figure out how to squeak past No. 17 Houston and win their first game in nearly a month on Friday, November 13 (10:15 p.m. ET, ESPN). Another loss will drop the Buffs out of postseason contention for the third time in Sanders' tenure.

#2839. Cade Cunningham scores 52, Pistons beat Wizards 144-140 in double OT

WASHINGTON (AP) — Cade Cunningham scored a career-high 52 points and had 11 assists, and the Detroit Pistons outlasted Washington 144-140 in double overtime Thursday night after the Wizards twice extended the game with last-second shots.

Trae Young's 3-pointer at the buzzer forced the first overtime, and then rookie AJ Dybantsa's midrange effort with less than a second left sent the teams to another OT. But Cunningham quickly made a 3-pointer, and then Anthony Davis fouled out to give Detroit the upper hand.

It was still a two-point game in the final minute, but Cunningham scored from the baseline to make it 142-138 with 25.3 seconds left. Washington has lost six straight.

Detroit's Ausar Thompson had 17 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists for his first career triple-double.

Young had 37 points for the Wizards but shot just 8 of 23. Davis and Alex Sarr scored 30 each as the franchise had its first trio of 30-point scorers since Mike Davis, Earl Monroe and Gus Johnson for the Baltimore Bullets on Nov. 18, 1969.

Young had 14 assists, two more than Washington's whole team managed in a loss at Indiana the previous night.

Cunningham's previous career high was 46 points, just over a year ago — and also against Washington. He became the first NBA player with 50 points, 10 assists and no turnovers since the league began tracking turnovers in 1977-78, according to OptaSTATS.

Detroit beat the Wizards for the second time in four games. The Pistons overcame Davis' 44 points to win Monday, and Washington looked ready to end its skid when it scored the first seven points of the first overtime Thursday to lead 128-121. Then Cunningham rallied Detroit.

PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Tyrese Maxey scored 27 points, Joel Embiid had 20 and Philadelphia beat Toronto while playing without LeBron James.

James (back) was ruled out earlier Thursday, missing his third game of the season.

Jaylen Brown added 18 points for Philadelphia, which improved to 10-3. The 76ers rebounded from Tuesday's 123-101 loss to Jayson Tatum and the Celtics in Brown's first game against his former team.

RJ Barrett scored 31 points and Immanuel Quickley added 25 for the short-handed Raptors, who have lost four of five.

Embiid (foot) was upgraded from questionable to available before tipoff. The 76ers got a scare in the first quarter when Embiid crumpled to the court after colliding with Quickley, clutching his right knee. But Philadelphia's 7-foot center returned later in the period to loud cheers from the home crowd.

The Raptors, playing without Kawhi Leonard (knee) for the 10th straight game and Scottie Barnes (groin) for the fourth consecutive contest, led by as many as 16 points in the opening half.

MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — LaMelo Ball made six 3-pointers and finished with 22 points and a season-high nine assists, and Minnesota beat Dallas for its most lopsided victory of the season.

Bones Hyland scored 24 points off the bench to lead the Timberwolves, who won their fifth straight game. Ayo Dosunmu added 18 points, Jaden McDaniels had 16 and Jonathan Kuminga had 14 points and eight rebounds.

Minnesota shot 61% in the first half to build a 15-point advantage, then blew it open by outscoring Dallas 36-17 in the third quarter to open a 103-69 lead.

Zaccharie Risacher scored 22 points off the bench for the Mavericks, who had their three-game winning streak snapped. Cooper Flagg, who had 43 against Indiana in his last game, was held to 12 points and Kyrie Irving had just 10.

The Wolves beat the Mavs for the seventh straight time and did it easily. Their previous largest margin of victory in a game this season was 25 points and their 44-point lead in the fourth quarter was their biggest at any point this season.

PHOENIX (AP) — Devin Booker had 30 points, seven assists and three steals, and Phoenix beat Charlotte.

Miles Bridges got the win in his first meeting against his former team as the Suns won for the fourth time in five games after a 1-5 start. Dillon Brooks added 15 points and Collin Gillespie had 13 for the Suns.

Bridges finished with 11 points and six rebounds. The No. 12 pick in the 2018 draft spent his first seven seasons in Charlotte, where he is third in team history in points, before being dealt to Phoenix in a deal that sent Grayson Allen and Royce O'Neale to the Hornets.

Coby White scored 21 points and Naz Reid had 16 for shot 6 for 18 from the field for the Hornets. Allen had 14 points and Christian Anderson finished with 13.

Booker's 3-pointer gave Phoenix a 97-91 lead with 28 seconds left but O'Neale converted a four-point play that cut it to two. Bridges made two free throws and Booker added two more after a steal as the Suns held on.

Booker scored 13 points as Phoenix took a 28-22 lead after one quarter, and the Suns extended it to 48-31 when Bridges capped a 15-4 run with a layup midway through the second. Charlotte closed well and cut it to 55-50 at halftime on Allen's 3-pointer.

#2835. How early-season shot selection shifts are impacting fantasy basketball value

We're far enough into the season to notice something useful, as long as we're careful about what we're measuring. Scoring averages and shooting percentages can swing a lot over the first few weeks. Where a player takes his shots tends to settle faster, so it's a better place to start.

In testing this for 2025-26, Tall Order Digital found that among 156 qualifying players, shot-zone shares over the first four games correlated with the rest of the season at 0.72 to 0.86 (a perfect match would be 1.0). Field-goal percentage correlated at just 0.46.

To see what the shifts are doing to fantasy basketball value, I've listed each player's preseason ADP next to his current 9-cat rank (through Nov. 11). Shot data is Basketball-Reference totals as of Nov. 11, compared with last season or a career mark.

Luka Dončić and De'Aaron Fox are ranked higher than where they were drafted, and Michael Porter Jr. has climbed despite scoring less. In all three cases, the revised shot profiles are landing and netting positive results.

He's launching 13.4 3s a game, up from 10.8 last season (which led the NBA). His 3-point share has risen from .476 to .549, and last year's .476 was already a career high. The bigger move is at the rim, where his share has dropped from .076 to .060. He's making 40.8% of his 3s and averaging 38.6 points in 11 games.

Fox is getting to the line far more often. He's attempted 53 free throws on 111 field-goal attempts, a free-throw rate of .477, compared with .235 last season and a .316 career mark. His career high is .420, set in 2019-20, so this is a new peak.

It isn't coming from more shots at the rim, though. His rim share is flat (.207 vs .201). What changed is the middle of the floor. Shots from 3-10 feet jumped from .204 to .315 of his attempts, while long twos nearly vanished (.067 to .018). He's also attempting 3.1 3s a game, down from 5.5, so his average shot is 12.4 feet from the basket instead of 14.4.

He's traded long twos and 3s for more floaters and short jumpers, and the whistle is doing the rest. He's backing it up with 51% shooting and 6.2 assists, though his scoring is 14.2 points, down from 18.6.

Porter is taking 3s on .615 of his attempts, up from .506 last season. He had never topped .556 in a season. His free-throw rate has climbed from .237 to .349, and his 10-to-16-foot share has collapsed from .075 to .018. He's averaging 21.5 points, below last season's 24.2, yet he's still up five spots in his draft position. A more interesting shot profile doesn't automatically mean more points. Playing alongside a player like Julius Randle likely also affects how a player navigates getting shots up.

These two are still scoring, but their rank has dropped since they were drafted. A new shot mix doesn't always show up the same way in the box score.

Durant is a free-throw story. His FTr has risen from .339 to .582 (92 attempts in 12 games, 7.7 a game), above his previous career best of .523 in 2012-13 and his .392 career mark. His 3-point volume has fallen from 5.8 a game to 3.8, and he's turning it over 3.3 times a game. Durant is at 20.9 points on 49% shooting. Having Fred VanVleet back and running more offense through Alperen Şengün is putting less dependency on Durant – which is probably a good thing in the long run. Fantasy-wise, Jabari Smith Jr. and Şengün's growth has Durant adjusting his shot profile, which could lessen his value as a scorer.

Gilgeous-Alexander's rim share has fallen from 22.8% to 13.1% and his 10-to-16-foot share has risen from .273 to .303. His 3s are up to .292 on 6.7 attempts a game from .226 on 4.4 last season. SGA's free-throw rate has dropped from .465 to .339. He's still scoring 29.7 a night, so this is a small slide from a very high perch.

That's an observable redistribution that likely comes down to how much attention he's drawing without co-stars Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren to balance out the Thunder's offensive attack. SGA is having to settle for more contested shots and rely more on his jumper. SGA has proven to be one of the most efficient guards in the league, but fantasy managers may have to accept that this could be a down season. He's shooting 45.6% from the field as of Wednesday.

This is where the shot shift is costing the most fantasy value. A big jump in one kind of shot usually takes a few weeks to settle and the efficiency tends to lag the volume. Whether that's what's happening here, or whether the new role simply isn't a good fit, is something we'll know more as we move further into the season.

In 10 games with Orlando, 100 of his 148 attempts have been 3s: 67.6%. His 3-point share had slid from .543 as a rookie to .354 last season, against a .441 career mark. His two-point attempts have fallen from 9.5 a game to 4.8 this season. His average shot distance is 23.4 feet, up from 13.5.

The results haven't been good: 39.2% from the field and 18.0 points a game, down from 20.1. The key question is whether Orlando keeps asking him to operate on such a narrow diet. If it does, last season's scoring profile may be the wrong baseline even after his shooting recovers.

Markkanen has the second-biggest 3-point jump on this list, making up .646 of his attempts, up from .402 last season. His previous career high was .570 in 2024-25. His rim share has halved, from .210 to .106, and his average shot distance has gone from 13.9 feet to 18.9. And now, he'll miss at least a month with two non-displaced fractures in his shooting hand.

He's scoring 18.0 points a game on 39% shooting, down from 26.7 in 42 games last season. A bigger share of 3s didn't produce more points here, at least so far.

Buzelis is a different case from the others in this group, because his shot mix barely changed. His 3s are .520 of his attempts, almost identical to last year's .514. What changed is how many shots he's taking. He's down from 12.5 field-goal attempts a game to about 9.8, with both his 3s (6.4 to about 5.1) and his twos (6.1 to about 4.7) falling, and his minutes slipped from 29.2 to 26.3.

His free-throw rate jumped from .247 to .429, but that's partly a smaller denominator. He's getting to the line about 4.2 times a game, up from 3.1, on far fewer shots. The extra trips haven't made up for the lost volume. He's shooting 43% with 2.8 turnovers, and he's ranked 226th. A higher free-throw rate doesn't help much when the shots aren't there to begin with. Caleb Wilson has a fractured hand and is reportedly expected to miss 4-6 weeks, so expect Buzelis to see a short-term boost in his volume.

Shot diets settle faster than shooting percentages, and that's the lens for this group. Bane and Markkanen have the clearest case: 3s are 68% and 65% of their shots, and that's likely to stick, while their 39% shooting is the part more likely to improve. More 3s  also means a lower field-goal percentage but more 3PM, so expect a trade-off in 9-cat rather than a clear gain.

Fox and Durant are getting to the line at career-high rates, which gives them some cushion on off nights, though it hasn't lifted either one's rank. Buzelis is the caution. His free-throw rate is up, but his shot volume is down, so the better rate hasn't helped his fantasy value.

Bet on the shot profile, then check whether the production is catching up.

#2834. Rangers Predicted to Land Three-Time All-Star in Massive Move

The Texas Rangers missed the playoffs again this past season, marking the third straight year without a trip to the dance.

Since the Rangers won the World Series in 2023, it has been tough sledding for this organization, with the team's core group struggling. But the Rangers did fight up until the final day of the regular season, falling just short of a playoff spot.

So, as the offseason continues, this team has a lot of work to do. Texas has a good foundation, but the roster needs some tweaks around the star players.

With the Rangers' desire to get back to the playoffs next year, this front office will be looking at bringing in talent. One name that could make a lot of sense is Gleyber Torres, who has been with the Detroit Tigers over the last few seasons.

MLB analyst Tim Kelly of Bleacher Report predicted that Torres would land with the Rangers this offseason. The contract projection came in at one year, worth $12 million, with a $15 million mutual option for 2028.

"A left oblique strain limited Torres to just 96 games this past season. This followed a core muscle injury he played through, which eventually required offseason surgery in the second half of the 2025 campaign, when he posted just a .659 OPS after making his third career All-Star Game appearance. Torres is still only entering his age-30 season, but he broke into the league as a 21-year-old. These injuries must be a concern for potential suitors.

Still, Torres probably doesn't get enough credit for the player he is when healthy. No, he's never developed into the superstar he appeared poised to be when he homered 62 times in his first two MLB seasons with the Yankees. But he posted a .754 OPS between 2022 and 2025. In an era when baseball lacks quality right-handed hitters, there's still plenty of reason to be interested in Torres' services," Kelly wrote.

For the season with Detroit, Torres slashed 260/.364/.363 with eight home runs, 38 RBIs, and 57 walks drawn, while posting an OPS of .727. Torres has been an All-Star three times over his career, and he could be just what the Rangers need for 2027.

Texas has a nice core in place, but the team does need a little more around the edges of the roster to get back to the postseason. Bringing in someone like Torres could help, and if he can stay healthy, this could be a steal for the Rangers.

Torres does a lot of little things well, and he could bring more consistency to the Rangers' offense moving forward. This was a real problem this past year for Texas, and Torres could be a way to mitigate the issues.

The hope would be that Torres would be able to bounce back from the injury-filled season, which is why Texas would give him a one-year deal with an option for 2028. But Torres could be one of the more underrated signings from the upcoming offseason, and the Rangers do need more players like this for the roster.

#2833. Cleveland Browns defense starting to show some cracks in the armor

The Cleveland Browns defense has been feeling the pressure through the first nine weeks of the season.

Following the complete team meltdown in Week 1 against Jacksonville, the defense has carried more than its share of the water each week.

It has become a familiar script: the defense keeps the Browns in the game while the offense bumbles its way through the first three quarters, only to catch fire when it appears all hope is lost to pull out a win.

At least that is how it has played out with Deshaun Watson as the starting quarterback. Unfortunately for the Browns, Watson was sidelined for last week's game against the New Orleans Saints with a concussion, so no winning comeback was to be found.

While everyone knows that playing the way the Browns have through the first nine games is not sustainable, most weeks it felt that way given the way the defense was playing.

But the strain has started to show on the defense over the past few weeks; in the previous three games, they have allowed an average of 24.7 points and 167 rushing yards per game.

So what can the defense do to get itself right and help the Browns avoid heading into the bye week on a three-game losing streak?

When asked about it on Thursday, defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg said it comes down to facing the challenge head-on and finding that extra bit of energy to make a difference:

"No one drive defines a game, and I think that's important for the whole team to know, and that's what Monk always talks about. Whether it's starting fast, finishing faster, making the play at the end of the half, going in, getting a three and out after halftime. Each little six-second play defines the game.

"And then of course at the end of the game, great defenses try their butts off to finish. And during the week, I'm not going to get into what we do, but what I can promise you is we are always addressing whatever came up head-on, honestly, together, and figuring out the best ways, whether it's in a meeting, whether it's out at practice, whether it's a drill. We do all that, and our guys are bought into that, and it's really cool to see."

But what about the run defense? While the Browns have never really been stout against the run, being ranked No. 27 against it (130.6 yards per game) this season doesn't make life any easier.

The Texas don't present a daunting challenge as they are ranked No. 29 in rushing (87.1 yards per game), but neither did the Saints, and they ripped off 141 rushing yards.

Rutenberg went back to his standby answer when asked about what the coaches can do this week to get things back on track:

"Every week, whatever it is, we address it, like I always say, because that's just what football is. And in terms of the run defense, great run games are based on violence, which is what we're built off of. Discipline fits and straining of the ball. And we'll continue to preach our style of strain and violence and our style of the mind to do our best in the fits, practice it like we've been doing it, and continue to, whatever it is, take that approach in everything we're trying to fix."

The joy of being 5-2 and first in the AFC North has started to slip away over the past two weeks, and the defense has played a role in that.

This week presents another challenge, and if the Browns hope to enter the bye with a victory, they are going to need the defense to get back to its particular strain of violence when the Texans have the ball.

#2830. Yankees news: Corey Seager in trade rumors

MLB Trade Rumors | Darragh McDonald: The Yankees are seeking upgrades in several spots this offseason, and McDonald provides a useful overview of the latest rumblings of what they might do. Perhaps the most eye-catching name mentioned is Corey Seager, who Jon Heyman claims that the Yankees have talked to the Rangers about. Color me skeptical for a variety of reasons: Seager has full no-trade protection, and as an oft-injured middle infielder on the wrong side of 30, I'm not sure he's worth taking on the remainder of his contract, or shelling out prospect capital to get the Rangers to eat some of it. Elsewhere, the Yankees have been connected to Luis Arraez and Brandon Lowe at second base, and Carson Kelly at catcher. Of course, the CBA negotiations cast a pall of uncertainty over everything, and it's possible that the Yankees will stay put until a deal is within sight.

NJ.com | Randy Miller: The narrative around how Anthony Volpe turned his season around following his second minor-league stint in 2026 is a bit overblown – he had a 95 wRC+ from September 10 onwards, which is above his career average but still nothing to write home about – but it was nice to see him hit for a respectable average and regain his mojo defensively over the stretch run. Apparently, a talk with Scott Boras might have been the catalyst for Volpe's bounceback. Volpe reportedly reached out to Boras sometime this year to collect feedback about his game. Although it's not clear what advice was given, there's reason to believe Boras knows what he's talking about; before he became the game's premier agent, Boras was a second baseman in the St. Louis Cardinals' system. Evidently, Volpe must have appreciated the feedback, as he dropped his former agency, WME Sports, to sign with Boras Corp. just before the playoffs. One can only hope that Boras' Volpe-whispering powers will lead to an even better 2027 campaign from the embattled infielder.

MLB.com | Jim Callis: Finally, another story from the AFL; after stalling as a catching prospect, 24-year-old Antonio Gomez is now trying to make it as a flamethrowing reliever. The Yankees signed Gomez out of Venezuela in 2018 based on his arm strength, but while his defense progressed throughout the minors, his bat couldn't keep up. In 2025, the Yankees approached him about giving pitching a chance, and while the results haven't quite been there yet, the raw stuff is impressive – triple digits on his heater, with a mid-90s cutter, an upper-90s sinker, and a mid-80s slider. I have a soft spot for prospects with unusual development paths, so I'll be rooting for Gomez to harness his stuff.

#2827. Jim Harbaugh: Broncos took advantage of a loophole the NFL should not allow

Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh is not happy with the way the Broncos backed out of a trade for Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley, or with the NFL rules that allowed them to do so.

After agreeing to trade a fourth-round pick and a fifth-round pick for Henley, the Broncos told Chargers GM Joe Hortiz they couldn’t go through with it because Henley’s physical revealed concerns about his knee. The Broncos were still willing to trade for Henley, but wanted to give up less. Harbaugh believes physical exams should only be to determine whether or not the player is healthy, not to renegotiate trade terms.

“What happened with the trade? Here’s what I know, from talking to Joe: The Broncos based a pass-fail on a medical grade based on whether we would take less compensation, and we wouldn’t and we didn’t,” Harbaugh said. “In my opinion it’s one of those loopholes that the league should really look into, because it sets a bad precedent.”

Asked if it’s permitted for teams to renegotiate trades after the trade deadline, Harbaugh answered, “It shouldn’t be, but apparently it is. That’s why it’s a loophole, and teams should not have the ability to do that.”

Harbaugh said the Broncos offered to say Henley passed his physical, but only if the Chargers would take something less than the fifth-round pick the Broncos had agreed to.

“It’s a medical grade. It’s a pass-fail for a medical grade, and they told us they weren’t going to pass him if it’s a fourth and a fifth, which was agreed upon — they would not pass him for that. They would pass him for a fourth and a fill in the blank. I don’t know what to call that, but that’s what it is,” Harbaugh said.

Harbaugh is right that the NFL has set a bad precedent. By allowing teams to renegotiate trade terms after the deadline, the NFL is incentivizing teams to engage in chicanery on physical exams to squeeze their trade partners into taking less favorable deals. The Chargers refused to budge, but the NFL rules shouldn’t have put the Chargers in a position where they had to make that decision.

The Nuggets run a tight rotation, and not much has changed since last week. DeMar DeRozan is seeing his minutes trend down a bit as the core group gets more usage and Spencer Jones returned from his injury. DeRozan figures to be just an ancillary piece on this team, barring injury.

The Pistons are another team with a narrow and consistent rotation. Isaiah Joe and Jalen Duren both remain sidelined, but Duren has begun on-court activities, so he could return from his hamstring injury in 2-3 weeks.

Obviously the big news for the Warriors is last night's injury to Stephen Curry, which I wrote about on the website today. With Gary Payton II also out, Brandon Williams suffering a hamstring injury, and both Moses Moody and Jimmy Butler recovering from knee surgeries, the Warriors are very short-handed. We should expect to see a bump in minutes for De'Anthony Melton.

With Steven Adams and Clint Capela sidelined by injuries, the Rockets may have the narrowest rotation in the league. It seems that both players could return this weekend, so we'll see what that does to the frontcourt minutes in Houston.

With Tyrese Haliburton (hamstring) still sidelined for another two weeks, the Pacers are relying a lot on Andrew Nembhard and Aaron Nesmith. The issue is that Nesmith left Wednesday's game with knee soreness and did not return. If he were to miss time, Kelly Oubre Jr. would figure to step into a larger role.

We might be getting closer to seeing Brandon Ingram take the court for the Clippers, but that time has not yet come. That leaves the Clippers in a precarious situation. Brook Lopez's return has meant fewer minutes for Isaiah Jackson, and Derrick Jones Jr. has been playing big minutes alongside Darius Garland. There's not a lot to get excited about here.

Walker Kessler has been a tremendous addition to the Lakers, and I covered his success in a video this week. He's the clear third option behind Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves, and the rest of the team is ancillary pieces. Reaves did have X-rays on his heel, which came back negative, but he could still miss some time. Collin Sexton also had to get stitches in his forehead on Wednesday, so he may miss a game or two as that heals. If both Reaves and Sexton are out, that would lead to a bigger role for Quentin Grimes.

Things are status quo from Memphis right now. Javon Small has moved into a role in the rotation, which has impacted the minutes for Cedric Coward, and Isaiah Stewart sat out for two games earlier in the week. It's possible that Kris Murray has just been phased out of the rotation.

The Heat have a very narrow rotation, and there is little to be excited about except for consistent minutes for Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo. Bobby Portis Jr. has seen his minutes trend down, and Andrew Wiggins doesn't seem likely to supplant Pelle Larsson from the starting lineup. Klay Thompson is playing a lot of minutes, but he's not the same player he was a few years ago.

I mentioned last week that Kel'el Ware and Ryan Rollins were getting far fewer minutes than I expected, and that has continued. I see no reason why the Bucks will change things up now, even if they should. Brayden Burries has been stepping into a bigger role in the starting lineup and is delivering, which I discussed in a video this week.

As the Timberwolves adjust to life without both Anthony Edwards and Donte DiVincenzo, they have given more minutes to Trey Lyles and Jaylen Clark. Terrance Shannon Jr. also missed a couple of games over the weekend but returned earlier this week. The Timberwolves are going to play their starting five for as many minutes as they can every night.

The Pelicans have a deep rotation but none of it is that exciting. Dejounte Murray returned from his brief absence, but Jeremiah Fears continues to play a much larger role in this offense. Jordan Poole is now back and in the mix, but Bennedict Mathurin suffered a thumb sprain and could miss some time.

The big story in New York is that Landry Shamet has seemingly supplanted Mikal Bridges in the rotation. Bridges will start and play minutes early, but he has seen very little time on the court in the second half and played just 17 minutes in each of the last two games. Deuce McBride and Tyler Kolek are also seeing more minutes as Bridges' role shrinks for the time being until he can get back on track. Josh Hart missed two games earlier in the week but returned on Wednesday.

We know how many injuries the Thunder are dealing with, but they got some reinforcements by trading for last year's Kings first-round pick Nique Clifford. Clifford figures to play just 15-20 minutes a game for the Thunder, but that is a locked-in part of the rotation. It's also a valuable role with Ajay Mitchell now dealing with a sprained ankle. Aday Mara has stepped into a bigger role without Chet Holmgren and looked really good in his rookie season.

The Magic continue to be one of the most injury-plagued teams. After dealing with injuries to Jalen Suggs and Paolo Banchero, the Magic now have Tristan da Silva out with a calf injury. That should lead to more minutes for Jase Richardson in the short term, but the usage will fall to Franz Wagner and Anthony Black.

We knew these 76ers would battle some injuries during the season, and it's starting now. LeBron James is out on Thursday with a back injury, and Joel Embiid could miss this game with a foot injury. None of those figure to be major injuries, but with Dominick Barlow also still sidelined, it makes the 76ers just a little bit thinner than they'd like to be.

Should the Suns play Collin Gillespie more? Yes, they need a true point guard. Will they? No, it doesn't seem like they will. Ryan Dunn has seen his minutes tick up, but this is an offense without a true floor general, and the results have been what you'd expect.

With Ja Morant and Shaedon Sharpe sidelined, we've seen an uptick in minutes for Chris Youngblood. However, Youngblood missed Wednesday's game, which led to increased minutes for Damian Lillard and Jrue Holiday. The Trail Blazers would rather not have to consistently play both of those veterans over 30 minutes per game.

Keegan Murray returned from his ankle injury and is right back to his normal role in the offense. Precious Achiuwa left Tuesday's game with a leg injury, but Dylan Cardwell was taking a lot of his minutes before that happened as well. Cardwell played 29 minutes in that game and should see his minutes totals rise because of his rebounding prowess.

The Spurs are relatively healthy and very good. Devin Vassell is out with an adductor injury, and Tobias Harris remains sidelined with a calf injury, but both of them could suit up by the end of the week. The rest is status quo,

Collin Murray-Boyles missed one game earlier this week, but he has played a bigger role with Kawhi Leonard sidelined and Scott Barnes also out with a groin injury. Alijah Martin has played more as a result of Barnes' injury, but it's not expected to sideline Barnes for too long.

The Jazz just lost Lauri Markkanen to a fractured hand after already losing Jaren Jackson Jr. to a knee injury. With Jusuk Nurkic also out with a toe injury, the Jazz are going to rely heavily on Darryn Peterson, Ace Bailey, and Keyonte George over the next few weeks. Jaxson Hayes also played 30 minutes in the first game without Markkanen, so expect that to continue.

With Justin Champagnie sidelined, the Wizards are running a bit of a shorter rotation. It's the same key names, and we should assume little will change if not for injury. Anthony Davis missed two games last week, which allowed Alex Sarr and Will Riley to play more minutes, but Davis has been great when he's on the court.

#2822. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2820. J.B. Bickerstaff Calls Out Pistons’ Terrible Defense After Cade Cunningham’s Historic 52-Point Game

Cade Cunningham led the Detroit Pistons to a 144-140 win over the Washington Wizards tonight with a historic 50+ point game. He finished with 52 points, 11 assists, five rebounds, one steal, and one block, shooting 16-25 from the field (64.0% FG) and 3-5 from beyond the arc (60.0% 3P).

Cunningham is now the only player in NBA history to have 50+ points and 10+ assists with zero turnovers in a single game.

After the game, head coach J.B. Bickerstaff praised Cade Cunningham's leadership on offense but did not seem pleased that the Pistons allowed the Wizards to score 140 points.

"It speaks to who he is; the more you're around him, the more you respect him for who he is and what his abilities are. To be able to do what he does when the moment gets called on, it's unique, and it's special. He never ceases to amaze. He just understands what it takes to get it done and has all the abilities to make those things happen," Bickerstaff said initially.

"The efficiency of it, taking care of the ball, sharing the ball. The ball is in his hands so much versus so many different covers and actions against him, but I thought he just made the right play over and over again," Bickerstaff later added on Cunningham's zero turnovers tonight.

A reporter then asked the Pistons' head coach what he thought about the team's resiliency in a double overtime win tonight.

"I told the guys I was proud of their resolve; I respect their resolve," he said.

"But we made too many mistakes to put ourselves in that position. We hold ourselves to a higher standard. In certain moments, we have to be able to generate a stop; we've got to be able to trust each other. Tonight I thought we made too many mistakes in those moments."

"We didn't pay attention to the details," he added about allowing Trae Young to make the buzzer-beating three-point shot to tie the game in regulation.

"It was bad. It was terrible. We were not up to our standard defensively," he later added. "Everything was bad."

There is a reason why the Pistons are currently one of the best defenses in the league, with the second-best defensive rating right now (107.9), just inches behind the Celtics (107.6).

Despite witnessing a historic offensive performance, J.B. Bickerstaff demands perfection on both ends of the floor from his team. So that reaction seems justifiable.

The Pistons have now improved to 8-3 for the season and are third in the Eastern Conference. They now move on to face the Heat on Saturday, November 14.

That will be a clash of two defensive powerhouses. It will certainly be interesting to see what adjustments J.B. Bickerstaff makes to their defensive strategies.

#2816. Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong shares classy message after beating Shohei Ohtani for NL MVP

Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong shares classy message after beating Shohei Ohtani for NL MVP appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Pete Crow-Armstrong may have dethroned Shohei Ohtani in the National League MVP race, but the Chicago Cubs star made sure to give the Los Angeles Dodgers superstar his due.

Crow-Armstrong was named the unanimous winner of the 2026 NL MVP award on Thursday, with Ohtani finishing second after winning the honor in each of the last two seasons. Speaking on MLB Network after the announcement, the 24-year-old reflected on being mentioned in the same breath as the two-way star.

"Being mentioned in conversations with, you know, one of the best pitchers in the sport, but also one of the best hitters, a World Series champion, and arguably the biggest part of that," Crow-Armstrong said.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"It's not like we're racing and going up against each other every day. But I think it's just the fact that I want to be better than I was the day before. And really, that's been all that I've needed to motivate myself with for really as long as I can remember."

That drive showed up all season long. Crow-Armstrong played in all 162 games and led the NL in home runs (45), OPS (.943) and WAR (9.8), while also swiping 41 bases to join the 40-40 club.

The two-time MLB All-Star also credited the people around him in the Cubs clubhouse, including manager Craig Counsell and teammates Alex Bregman and Nico Hoerner.

"I've been lucky to be in really good clubhouses my first, you know, parts of four seasons up here. They give me patience and a lot of runway to be myself and succeed that way," he said.

Crow-Armstrong now joins a list of Cubs MVPs that includes Ernie Banks, Ryne Sandberg, Andre Dawson, Sammy Sosa and Kris Bryant. He singled out the late Sandberg, who supported him while battling cancer.

"He made himself available for a lot of us over the last few years through chemo and everything. He was hugely important to the last few years of my life," Crow-Armstrong said.

He added that he had spoken with Bryant earlier in the day. "I'm happy to carry on their legacy," he said.
