#2812. Cunningham scores 52 as Pistons win double OT thriller against Wizards

Cade Cunningham racked up 52 points as the Detroit Pistons edged a double-overtime thriller 144-140 against Washington on Thursday.

The Wizards twice extended the game with clutch scores in the dying seconds but could not repeat the trick a third time as the Pistons held their nerve to claim an epic road win.

Cunningham became the first player in NBA history to score 50 points and add 10 assists with zero turnovers, while Ausar Thompson had a triple-double with 17 points, 11 assists and 11 rebounds.

The Wizards had three starters scoring 30-plus points -- Trae Young, Anthony Davis and Alex Sarr -- but it was not enough to prevent Washington's sixth defeat in a row.

"Two overtimes, it was just going to come down who wanted it more, who had more in the tank," said Cunningham.

"I'd bet on my team any day. So great win for us."

In a back-and-forth game featuring 20 lead changes, Detroit started slow but built a double-digit lead early in the second half.

It was slowly whittled down by Washington, but the Pistons were clinging on to their lead when Cunningham was fouled at 119-118 with less than two seconds remaining.

Cunningham sank both free throws, but Trae Young made a nerveless trey right at the buzzer to force overtime.

The Wizards raced 128-121 up but Cunningham would not quit.

He made a three-pointer with 30 seconds left to level the score, then set up Duncan Robinson for what appeared to be another. A video replay ruled Robinson's toe was on the line, and Detroit had only a two-point lead.

That proved crucial as Young set up this year's top draft pick AJ Dybantsa, who forced a second overtime period with a pull-up jump shot.

Cunningham made a fadeaway shot for a four-point lead with 25 seconds left, and this time the Wizards could not conjure a third comeback.

Young missed two three-point efforts, with Washington settling for two free throws, but were unable to score in their final possession.

Tyrese Maxey powered Philadelphia to its latest comeback victory, scoring 27 points as the Sixers shrugged off a slow start and the absence of LeBron James to beat the Toronto Raptors 123-112.

Maxey added eight assists, linking up seamlessly with Joel Embiid, who briefly left the court early with a knee injury but returned to add 20 points.

The Sixers had trailed by 17 points in the first quarter, immediately following Embiid's absence, but rallied for their fifth double-digit comeback this season.

"We'll take it. I mean, extreme professional win by us. We stayed with it. Didn't start out great, but it was a good win," said Maxey.

"We played together the last seven years, so I kind of know where he's going to be, he knows where I'm going to be at, and it's good for us," he said of his partnership with 2023 MVP Embiid.

Veteran James, who turns 42 next month, was ruled out of Thursday's clash to manage a lower back issue.

Philadelphia moved to 10-3, just half a game back from the 10-2 Boston Celtics atop the Eastern Conference.

The Minnesota Timberwolves thrashed Dallas 133-94 while Devin Booker's 30 points helped the Phoenix Suns overcome Charlotte 101-96.

#2807. DeMarvion Overshown didn't know inactive players couldn't celebrate on the field

The Cowboys had 14 accepted penalties for 153 yards in the 27-23 win over the Colts. One of them was called unacceptable and undisciplined by Cowboys executive vice president Stephen Jones.

Linebacker DeMarvion Overshown, who was inactive and dressed in street clothes, came onto the field to celebrate after Quinnen Williams forced a Jonathan Taylor fumble that Shemar James returned to the Dallas 30. Overshown was penalized 15 yards, with referee Clay Martin saying, “After the play, unsportsmanlike conduct by Dallas. We have non-uniformed player in blue sweats and a stocking cap come onto the field to celebrate. That’s a 15-yard penalty.”

Overshown apologized to head coach Brian Schottenheimer and his teammates.

“At the end of the day, I talked to Schotty about it,” Overshown said Thursday, via Calvin Watkins of the Dallas Morning News. “I apologized about it. It was definitely in the moment, but earlier I had said that as a defense, we’re going to start celebrating more, getting takeaways. And I was just caught in the moment. So you can laugh at it now, because we won the game, but in the moment, fourth quarter, tied ball game or close ball game, you don’t want a 15-yard penalty from a guy, especially that’s not even playing. So that’s a lesson learned.”

Overshown said he didn’t know the rule until linebacker Dee Winters started yelling at him, which should prompt questions about why Overshown didn’t know the rule. But he defended Schottenheimer and said he accepted his “butt chewing.”

“It’s not an indictment on Schotty. It’s on me as a player. I own it,” he said.

#2805. Cam Skattebo Illness Update: Giants RB Sick on Sideline During Commanders Game

The hot start by New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo in Thursday night's Week 10 game against the Washington Commanders was welcome after he missed a Week 9 win over the Philadelphia Eagles with a hamstring injury.

What wasn't welcome was the mess Skattebo made on the Giants sideline in the first half when he came off the field, sat down, and threw up everywhere.

NFL on Prime sideline reporter Kaylee Hartung said Skattebo covered up his "mess" with a towel as trainers came over to check on him, and he was seen smiling afterward.

Skattebo had 61 yards from scrimmage in the first quarter and got sick after Giants kicker Dominic Zvada missed a 33-yard chip-shot field goal — the Giants trailed 3-0 early in the second quarter.

"Cam Skattebo threw up on the sidelines but is all smiles," NFL reporter Tanner Phifer wrote on his official X account on Thursday night.

"Cam Skattebo threw up on the sidelines, then covered it up with a towel," Underdog wrote on its official X account.

Skattebo returned to the game right after getting sick and scored a 1-yard touchdown late in the second quarter to give the Giants a 7-3 lead — followed by his signature backflip.

Steady and constant rain at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, all day leading up to kickoff put an extra spotlight on Skattebo as the Giants' top option at running back.

Players on the field and fans in the stands were asked to shelter in place just over an hour before the start of the game when lightning strikes were spotted in the area but the game was still able to start on time.

"Clearing the field at Giants Stadium for bad weather," NBC Sports' JP Finlay wrote on his official X account on Thursday night.

"EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Everybody take cover," NFL Network's Mike Garafolo wrote on X.

"Players are being instructed to vacate the field during early warmups due to severe weather in the area," The Athletic's Dan Duggan wrote on X. "Going to be interesting if the kickoff actually gets pushed back. Players have to get mandatory warmup time. Hearing the field will be cleared at least 30 mins but also seems like things are quite fluid."

The first-place Giants are 5-2-1 while the Commanders are 2-5-1 — the teams played to a now-infamous 27-27 overtime tie in Week 5.

Skattebo's career low point — so far — came in a 27-27 overtime time against the Commanders in Week 5.

Skattebo fumbled at the Commanders' 23-yard line with just under 2 minutes left in overtime, killing the Giants' chances of kicking a short, game-winning field goal.

After head coach John Harbaugh benched Skattebo in a Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints, he bounced back with the best game of his career in a Week 7 overtime win over the Houston Texans with 124 yards and 1 touchdown on just 17 carries — a whopping 7.3 yards per carry.

#2803. Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson undergoes surgery on fractured hand, reportedly out 4-6 weeks

The Chicago Bulls will reportedly be without rookie Caleb Wilson for a while. After suffering a fractured right hand on Wednesday, Wilson underwent successful surgery on Thursday and will miss four to six weeks, the Bulls announced.

Wilson was initially reported to be out for four-to-six weeks. The Bulls said he will be re-evaluated in three weeks.

The rookie suffered the injury during the second half of Wednesday's loss to the San Antonio Spurs, heading to the locker room in the third quarter. He was ruled out of the game before the start of the fourth quarter.

It was unclear when Wilson sustained the fractured, though the Bulls broadcast highlighted a play where Wilson's right hand got jammed against Victor Wembanyama's elbow.

Wilson, who was selected No. 4 overall out of North Carolina in June, was touted as a young player to help revive the Bulls. A dominant showing in the NBA Summer League boosted Wilson's profile ahead of the regular season.

So far, he has shown a lot of promise, averaging 18.9 points, 6.2 rebounds and 1.9 assists per game as a starting power forward.

However, Wilson has a history of hand injuries, fracturing each of his hands — his left hand in February and his right hand in March before the NCAA tournament — during his lone freshman season with the Tar Heels.

#2802. What changed? Rams make stunning Puka Nacua reversal just one day after McVay’s assurances

On Wednesday, Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay insisted the team had no plans to place star wide receiver Puka Nacua on injured reserve, citing what he called "roster semantics."

By Thursday afternoon, those semantics apparently went out the window.

The Rams announced they were placing Nacua on IR after all, guaranteeing their leading receiver will miss at least four games as he recovers from knee and toe injuries suffered during Sunday's 20-13 victory over the Washington Commanders.

"Puka [Nacua] with his knee/toe. We're not going to put him on IR because of some semantics with the roster and things like that, but he still is going to be out for an extended period of time," McVay said Wednesday. "It wasn't like any sort of new information."

Apparently, the roster math changed overnight.

Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua (12) warms up before a game against the Arizona Cardinals at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua reacts after winning an NFL football game against the Washington Commanders in Landover, Md., Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. AP Photo/Stephanie Scarbrough

Nacua will now be sidelined through the Rams' Dec. 13 showdown with the San Francisco 49ers, making their Dec. 20 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys his earliest possible return.

To fill the vacancy, Los Angeles promoted wide receiver Brennan Presley to the active roster and signed Tyler Scott to the practice squad.

But the decision carries consequences beyond losing Stafford's favorite target for the next month.

Under NFL rules, teams are limited to eight injured reserve return designations during the regular season. The Rams have already used three and are expected to need four more for Davante Adams, Kobie Turner, Terrance Ferguson and Nacua.

That would leave just one available designation for the remainder of the season.

Justin Dedich, Dean Connors and Jordan Whittington are also on injured reserve, meaning the Rams could eventually face some uncomfortable decisions about who gets another opportunity to play.

They could also preserve that final designation as insurance against another injury.

For a team already battered by injuries and desperately trying to keep its Super Bowl aspirations alive, every roster spot has now become precious.

#2799. Studs and duds from New York Giants' Week 10 loss to Washington Commanders

The New York Giants hoped to give their raucous fanbase a gift at MetLife Stadium on national television Thursday night. Instead, they helped the Washington Commanders salvage their sagging season.

With several opportunities for victory, the Giants played not to lose, and that passive approach cost them. Instead of going into the weekend riding high, they fall to 5-3-1 on the season with a game against the Jacksonville Jaguars looming.

Here's a look at some studs and duds from Thursday's 24-21 loss to the Commanders.

The Commanders had few answers for Likely, who caught nine of 11 targets for 127 yards, including a 66-yard touchdown that gave the Giants the lead in the second half. It was a Pro Bowl-caliber performance for the Giants' prized free-agent signing this year.

His 33-yard missed field goal attempt in the first quarter loomed large all game. When you lose by three, and you miss a chip shot, it hurts. Zvada's kickoff after the Giants took the lead in the early fourth quarter, which went out of bounds, was mistake number two. It didn't matter in the overall scheme of things, but it was a mistake that could've been very costly.

The reserve defensive back had a signature game with six total stops, two passes defensed and an interception. The 5-foot-8 former Baltimore Raven made some key stops in the second half to keep Big Blue in the game.

For the second straight game, Nabers failed to reach the century mark in receiving yards. He caught five passes for just 44 yards on seven targets. The Giants' final offensive play was a downfield pass to Nabers, who was boxed out by a Commanders defender for a game-sealing interception.

A big comeback game for the second-year running back. Skattebo rushed 18 times for 78 yards with two touchdowns and added 44 more yards on three receptions.

The rookie had another productive game with 13 overall tackles (four solo) and has clearly become the Giants' best player on defense this season.

#2771. NBA suspends Rockets G Marcus Smart 3 games for throwing punch at Warriors' Charles Bassey

The NBA doesn't look kindly on players who throw punches during a game. Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart was suspended three games without pay by the NBA on Thursday after throwing a punch at Golden State Warriors center Charles Bassey during Wednesday's game.

In its statement, the league specifically says the punch made contact with Bassey's face. The suspension is set to cover Houston's games against the Utah Jazz on Friday, the Washington Wizards on Sunday and the Miami Heat on Monday.

The incident occurred in the third quarter of Houston's 115-108 win. With less than a minute to go in the quarter, Smart and Bassey appeared to exchange words on the court. Smart then threw a punch at Bassey right in front of an official.

Smart was assessed with a flagrant 2 foul and ejected from the contest. He had already exited the court by the time the officials announced the punishment.

Smart finished the game with 6 points, 2 rebounds and 1 assist.

Under NBA rules, Smart faced — at the minimum — a fine for the flagrant foul and a suspension for throwing a punch, which comes with a minimum one-game ban in the NBA rulebook:

Any player who throws a punch, whether it connects or not, has committed an unsportsmanlike act. He will be ejected following confirmation during review by instant replay and suspended for a minimum of one game.

The incident occurred after Smart and Bassey got tangled up during a rebound attempt. Following the contest, Rockets coach Ime Udoka said Smart confronted Bassey after the Warriors center wrapped up Smart's elbow on the play. Bassey reportedly told Smart "what are you gonna do," leading to the attempted punch.

Bassey, meanwhile, had something to say about what he called "fake toughness" from Smart:

"He's been playing dirty the whole game," Bassey said, according to Yahoo Sports' Kelly Iko. "I don't think he was trying to play, I think he was trying to get kicked out of the game."

Smart's absence didn't hurt the Rockets too badly in the end, as the team still managed to pull off a win. It probably helped that Warriors star Stephen Curry sustained an oblique tear early in the contest, missing much of the game.

Curry is now expected to miss some time with the oblique tear.

#2770. How Hockey Proves Class and Sportsmanship Still Have a Place in Professional Sports

It is the only major team sport that allows fighting. Hockey is played with helmets, sticks and blades. Players are checked, slashed, tripped, hooked and held. It is a game defined by blood on the ice, toothless competitors and violent collisions. And, oh yeah, it might just be the last bastion of class in professional sports.

In a sports world where Pat McAfee is swears, Joe Buck and Troy Aikman are openly at odds, and Jaylen Brown refuses to shake hands with longtime teammate Jayson Tatum; hockey is actually carrying the torch for dignity in athletics.

I watched the 2026 Hockey Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony this past week, which was simulcast on NHL Network and TSN. The inductees list included star after star after star.

Patrice Bergeron, a 19-season Boston Bruins center, multiple award winner and 2011 Stanley Cup champion. Cindy Curley, a women's hockey trailblazer who scored a record 23 points at the 1990 IIHF Women's World Championship. Carey Price, the winningest goaltender in the storied history of the Montreal Canadiens.

Pekka Rinne, a Nashville Predators icon and the winningest Finnish goaltender in NHL history. Keith Tkachuk, a tough yet skilled player who helped establish the power forward position. Brian Burke, the gruff, hard-edged executive and television commentator.

The ceremony offered a clear demonstration of why class remains alive and well in the National Hockey League. But it certainly isn't the only reason.

Let's start with the surface stuff. Many of today's sports television personalities dress like fans who just got escorted out of the arena. NHL play-by-play announcers and color analysts, however, take a different approach. These men and women are almost always look the part in sport coats, fine suits or dresses. High dollar shirts and ties.

Their attire is more suited for a fashion show than a faceoff.

In 2020, when the erudite Mike 'Doc' Emrick decided to retire as the lead play-by-play announcer for the NHL on NBC, he left a void in the hockey broadcast booth. Thankfully, that void has been filled by the likes of Kenny Albert, Sean McDonough, Eddie Olczyk, P.K. Subban, Kevin Weekes, Steve Levy and many others. Each bringing their own elegance and professionalism to the role.

Conversely, the NFL has gone in a different direction. Personalities like McAfee and ESPN's Jason Kelce know football. But their personalities and broadcasting styles are often loud, boisterous and animated. Moreover, sports media has become a place where excitement often surpasses experience.

Another example of what separates the NHL from other professional sports is its postseason. During the NHL playoffs, officials tend to call fewer penalties. Thus allowing these incredibly strong athletes to skate harder and play a more physical game.

What happens at the end of every playoff series? Two teams that just spent four to seven games beating the living heck out of each other meet at center ice and shake hands. That's right. The same hand that formed a fist and made a violent connection with an opponent's jaw is the one that reaches out to that opponent with grace and sportsmanship.

Perhaps tennis, where players meet at center court after a match and shake hands. But nothing compares to getting smacked in the face by a piece of hard rubber traveling at 100 mph, especially when the alternative is getting nicked in the knee by a wayward fluorescent green Dunlop.

There is a long-running belief in sports media that hockey players are among the most accommodating athletes when it comes to interviews and media availability. We see plenty of clips of coaches and athletes in other sports ducking reporters or being downright rude to them. In turn, NHL players tend to be available and accommodating.

They seem to have retained the seemingly lost qualities of politeness and cooperation.

The 2026 Hockey Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony showcased both sides of hockey. You had players like Bergeron and Price, soft-spoken beacons of class who thanked their teammates. Shunned the spotlight and essentially gave everyone else credit for their brilliant careers.

Then you had Burke, who entered in the Builder category. The Minnesota native's speech was more like a Don Rickles roast. At one point, he ran through the numerous teams, organizations and television networks he had worked for and joked, "A lot of thanks for people who fired me. I don't know why I'm doing it."

Each of the Hall of Fame inductees devoted more time to thanking others than congratulating themselves. Isn't that refreshing in today's world of look-at-me clicks, likes and follows?

The NHL has always set the pace when it comes to identifiable players. A lunch-pail attitude and a basic gentility that somehow coexists with bone-crushing hits and fisticuffs. Moreover, the sports world needs these dignified degenerates now more than ever.

These aren't NBA players who embrace load management. Or even baseball pitchers who consider 75 pitches or five innings a complete game. Hockey players don't break a nail and miss six weeks. They break a bone and return by the middle of the second period.

Perhaps no one exemplifies the class-and-crash dichotomy of the NHL more than 2026 Hall of Fame inductee Tkachuk. In addition, he ranks 36th all-time in goals with 536 and 41st in penalty minutes with 2,219. During his induction speech, he summed up the singular beauty of the NHL with a simple statement: "Our culture is the best in sports."

Then, Taylor offered a revealing introduction: "I'm not comfortable doing it, but I'm going to do what he asked."

Consider that arrangement. The personnel department makes a mistake. Its leader determines how the mistake should be portrayed. The coach delivers the explanation, acknowledges his discomfort and faces the questions.

Tobin was not made available to reporters. Apparently, taking responsibility can be delegated by Bengals management.

The Bengals reportedly agreed to send a sixth-round draft pick to Philadelphia for Ebiketie. But acquiring his contract also would have canceled the projected third-round compensatory pick associated with Trey Hendrickson's departure in free agency.

Over the Cap analyst Nick Korte publicly flagged that consequence. Shortly afterward, the Bengals backed out. NFL Network reported that the compensatory-pick issue caused the reversal.

Backing out was the right decision. Understanding the full price before reaching an agreement would have been better.

Taylor conveyed that the transaction proved more costly than initially anticipated and that the problem was on Cincinnati's end. That leaves an obvious question: How did the personnel operation get that far without accounting for a third-round pick?

Tobin should answer it himself. We have been here before with his absence.

After the November 2025 trade deadline, Enquirer columnist Jason Williams reported that the Bengals had not made Tobin available to explain their inactivity or answer for the roster's problems. Taylor was left to handle the questions while the executive responsible for assembling the team remained silent.

This week brought a particularly awkward variation: Taylor was expected to explain a front-office failure according to instructions from the front office.

Coaches answer publicly for play calls, clock management, preparation and losses. Players stand at their lockers and explain missed assignments. The personnel chief should be able to explain a transaction his department failed to complete.

Korte, meanwhile, deserves acknowledgment.

In 2024, he questioned Cincinnati's compensatory-pick award following Jessie Bates III's departure. The NFL subsequently acknowledged its own calculation error and upgraded a sixth-round selection to the third round. That was a league mistake, not another failed Bengals trade. But Korte's analysis again proved valuable to Cincinnati.

The Bengals have not confirmed whether Korte's post alerted them to the problem, though it has been reported that it did. If so, a public thank-you would be appropriate.

More Dennis Doyle: Reds need to pay Sal Stewart before his price goes up | Opinion

Fans deserve more than an apology delivered through the coach. They deserve to know what went wrong and what will change.

He should have stepped forward to explain how it happened. That's what good organizations do.

#2759. Justin Jefferson: It's a joy to see Kirk Cousins take over as a leader

Kirk Cousins is back in Minnesota, and perhaps no one is more excited about that than Justin Jefferson.

The wide receiver had career highs in catches (128) and yards (1,809) and earned the NFL’s Offensive Player of the Year award in Cousins’ last full season with the Vikings in 2022.

Jefferson, though, said he has “no expectations.”

“It’s really just going out there and just executing our plays,” Jefferson said, via Kevin Seifert of ESPN. “It’s not really getting too juiced up about him being here or anybody being back there. It’s just all about understanding the plays that are being called, understanding the jobs that we have and executing our responsibilities. And just the plays that are there, and the plays that could be made, we just need to continue to just make those type of plays. And I’m pretty sure that the results would be a lot better.

“He just understands the game. He’s a guy that studies the game a lot. He understands how the defenses play, especially covering me. And he understands, the plays that we have called that are kind of my plays and he understands the timing and the windows to throw those type of plays, but he also doesn’t force those type of plays to me and he just lets the game come to me.”

Jefferson said it was “a joy to hear [Cousins] just take over and be a leader in the meeting room, on the field.”

“He’s being vocal,” Jefferson said. “Just making sure that everybody hears the plays that he’s talking about and the notes that he has for certain routes, certain plays. And he’s just making sure that everybody’s on the same page. So it’s definitely cool to hear that type of leadership and command. If you know Kirk, that’s pretty normal from him. So it’s definitely kind of cool him being back in that room and him taking that control.”

#2754. Mike Brown not ready to make a Mikal Bridges role change despite offensive struggles

Mikal Bridges is basically a starter in name only at the moment.

His minutes and production both resemble a bench player so far this season. It's really only his inclusion in the pregame introductions that represents his status as a starter.

But Knicks coach Mike Brown is not yet ready to make a change.

"Mikal is a starter, so it's not a question of that," Brown said. "Like a lot of players, they've had their good moments and their not-so-good moments. Mikal has a proven track record of playing at a pretty high level as a starter in this league. So for me to make a quote-unquote panic decision and change it, right now we're [11] games in or whatever we are, I'm not feeling it."

New York Knicks guard Mikal Bridges (25) reaches for the ball during the first quarter against the Cleveland Cavaliers, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in New York. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

Bridges played just 17 minutes in the Knicks' 115-107 loss to the Cavs Wednesday night at Madison Square Garden and only recorded two points. He was on the bench for the entirety of the fourth quarter.

For the season, Bridges is averaging 24.4 minutes per game — notably fewer than Landry Shamet's 25.9 minutes per game despite Shamet coming off the bench eight of the Knicks' 11 games.

Bridges' offensive struggles to start the year have resulted in Brown increasingly opting to go with Shamet or Miles McBride on the court, particularly to close games. Shamet and McBride have played 69 and 43 fourth-quarter minutes this year, respectively, compared to Bridges' 41. Bridges' 5.9 points per game are eighth most on the team, and he is shooting a woeful 32.9 percent from the field and 26.5 percent from 3-point range.

He has scored just four total points in fourth quarters this year — fewer than bench-warmers Pacôme Dadiet and James Wiseman, who usually only play in garbage time, have produced. It's half of what Dalton Knecht, who has played in just three games this year, has delivered in fourth quarters.

Brown's changing sentiment is telling. He began the year saying that his starting five was entrenched and that everyone else on the roster was fighting for minutes. Then, last week, he said that Shamet is "about as close to being a starter as you can imagine for us." And after Wednesday's game, Brown admitted that he feels a need to make room for Shamet and McBride.

New York Knicks head coach Mike Brown reacts on the baseline during the second quarter of an NBA game against the Milwaukee Bucks on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

Bridges can usually at least hang his hat on the defensive end, but that's an area in which Shamet and McBride are thriving as well. Brown has praised their point-of-attack defense and said that their tracking data has shown that Shamet has been their best pick-and-roll defender this season.

"We got two guys that are playing really well in Landry and Deuce," Brown said. "So it's hard. It's gonna be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal. And maybe even at times for Josh [Hart], because those two guys are playing at a pretty high level. Not just on the offensive end of the floor, but defensively too. … Landry and Deuce have been a big part of what we've done defensively. They're playing at a high level. I gotta keep trying to find ways to get those guys on the floor."

The Knicks have certainly been here before with Bridges. He went through significant slumps each of the past two regular seasons before coming up big in the postseason.

Last year, it reached a crescendo during the first round of the playoffs, when the Knicks fell to a 2-1 series deficit to the Hawks. Brown repeatedly sat Bridges in the second halves of those first three games and faced constant questions about replacing him in the starting lineup.

But Brown held firm with Bridges, who rewarded him by playing a key role in the championship run.

The Knicks are confident a similar bounce back is looming.

"No matter what's going on, with what people are saying or anything, the people in this room have his back night in and night out," Jalen Brunson said. "We see the work he puts into his game. We see the time that he puts in. When you're doing the right things day in and day out, things will eventually fall in your favor. So just giving him support, giving him confidence every single day, regardless of what the noise is on the outside. That's our brother, we're gonna keep it that way."

Warriors center Charles Bassey kept his hands down when Marcus Smart swung at him.

The incident came with 21 seconds left in the third quarter of Houston's 115-108 win over Golden State. Smart and Bassey got tangled up during a possession, then continued jawing as they ran back up the floor.

Golden State Warriors center Charles Bassey, left, and Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart, center, react during an NBA game in Houston, Nov. 11, 2026. AP Photo/Ashley Landis

Smart turned and threw a punch that grazed Bassey's nose. Officials assessed a Flagrant 2, and Smart walked off before they announced the ejection.

Bassey said afterward that Smart had been playing dirty throughout the game and dismissed the punch as "fake toughness."

Golden State Warriors center Charles Bassey, center left, is held back after a confrontation with Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart, center, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. AP Photo/Ashley Landis

#2749. Thursday Night Football: Stefon Diggs' late TD gives Commanders 24-21 win

With 3:27 remaining in Thursday’s game, the Giants lined up with Jameis Winston under center on fourth-and-1 from their own 11. The team’s backup quarterback, who runs the team’s quarterback sneaks, yelled, “Hut One. Hut Two. Hut Three. Who let the dogs out? Who, who, who, who?”

The Giants took a delay of game and then punted.

The Commanders got the last laugh, winning 24-21 on Stefon Diggs’ 32-yard touchdown with 57 seconds left. The Commanders are 3-5-1 and the Giants 5-3-1.

In an entertaining second half, the teams traded the lead four times.

The Giants took a 21-17 lead with 8:13 left on Isaiah Likely’s 66-yard catch-and-run.

The Giants then had back-to-back interceptions of Jayden Daniels. Safety Jevon Holland, who is having an All-Pro season, took the ball away from Chig Okonkwo at the 2-yard line with the Commanders on the Giants 24 with 5:27 left, and Ar’Darius Washington stepped in front of Okonkwo on fourth-and-2 at the Washington 45 with 2:15 left.

The Giants, though, couldn’t run out the clock, and the Commanders made the most of it. They needed only three plays to go 71 yards thanks to a questionable 33-yard pass interference penalty on Deonte Banks, who was covering Treylon Burks. Three plays later, Diggs scored.

The Giants reached the Washington 48 on their final drive, but J.J. McCarthy’s deep throw to Malik Nabers was intercepted by Rasul Douglas with 25 seconds left to end it.

The Giants outgained the Commanders 399 to 340, but missed a field goal and had two turnovers.

Daniels was 23-of-33 for 249 yards with three touchdowns and two interceptions. Rachaad White ran for 47 yards on 11 carries, and Diggs caught six passes for 83 yards. Antonio Williams and Ben Sinnott each caught a touchdown pass.

McCarthy was 23-of-36 for 293 yards with a touchdown and an interception. Cam Skattebo had 18 carries for 78 yards and two touchdowns and caught three passes for 44 yards, and Likely had nine receptions for 127 yards and a touchdown.

#2746. John Harbaugh expresses confidence in K Dominic Zvada

Giants rookie kicker Dominic Zvada has missed six field goals in nine games. He missed another on Thursday night, a 33-yarder.

While it happened in the first quarter and not on the final play, it stands out in a game that was decided by three points.

After New York’s 24-21 loss to the Commanders, Giants coach John Harbaugh was asked about his level of confidence in Zvada.

“Yeah, we’re confident,” Harbaugh said. “You know, you can’t — as soon as a guy doesn’t make a play, I mean, start firing people left and right. Especially your kicker who’s a rookie. So I’m confident that he’s gonna become a good kicker. I mean, if at some point in time, it doesn’t happen, it doesn’t happen.

“But I’m not gonna panic, you know, halfway through the season when the guy who’s made a bunch of kicks, if that’s what you’re inferring we should be doing.  So, you know, I mean, we’re just not gonna knee-jerk it like that. He’s gonna make kicks. He’s gonna make a lot of kicks, I believe in him.  I think he’s really good, really talented. And we’re gonna give him an opportunity to do it. It’s up to him to do it.”

That’s a fair assessment of a player who’s still new to the NFL. But a kicker has one job. If he can’t do it (especially from distances that should be automatic), at some point tough questions need to be asked.

Basically, how much time will Zvada get before Harbaugh decides it’s not going to happen? That remains to be seen, if Zvada keeps missing kicks he should be making.

#2744. Cris Collinsworth Makes Strong Statement on Bengals QB Joe Burrow

NBC Sports' Cris Collinsworth will call Sunday's biggest NFL game, as the Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) travel to the Queen City to face the Cincinnati Bengals (6-2) in an AFC North divisional showdown.

Pittsburgh won the first meeting over a month ago, 30-27, in a game that went right down to the wire.

Now, this one will be for the outright lead in the division. It also marks the first time Bengals star quarterback Joe Burrow will play a primetime home game against a division opponent. Every other time, he's had to go on the road.

On Thursday, Collinsworth joined First Word With James Rapien and shared his thoughts on Burrow.

"He works very hard at his craft and you can tell that. But he's basically taken this entire team on his shoulders," Collinsworth said. "And I think everybody down there would tell you that. And from just analyzing football, like in my mind, it's always been you've got to have a little bit of everything. You've gotta play defense, you've gotta be able to run it, you've gotta be able to throw it. But maybe it's like maybe they just do have to throw it…. why would you not give it to Joe Burrow and throw it every time cause they're just so good at it."

In his seventh season with Cincinnati, Burrow is on pace to have his best year yet. And he firmly has put himself in the MVP conversation without question.

He enters Sunday night completing 74.0% of his passes, which leads the NFL, for 2,386 yards and 23 touchdown passes, which also leads the league.

This week, he acknowledged the importance of the matchup against Pittsburgh and noted that it's one of the biggest games the Bengals have played as a franchise in quite some time.

"This is as big of a game as we've had here for awhile," Burrow said earlier this week. "Lost to them earlier in the season… for first place outright. Huge game."

#2742. The Three Point Stance: Purdue (3-6) vs. #16 Iowa (7-2)

Purdue will travel to take on the 16th ranked Iowa Hawkeyes in an effort to salvage a season that at one point seemed very promising at 3-3 following victories against Illinois and Minnesota. Head Coach Barry Odom will take on defensive play calling duties following a Sunday afternoon announcement that he had fired defensive coordinator Kevin Kane following a season of continued errors and fundamental mistakes. To get a victory would mean a seismic shift from what Purdue has been over the last several weeks but not out of the realm of possibility from what they have shown at times this season.

Iowa enters this game as a team on the fringe of consideration of a College Football Playoff invitation. Sitting at 7-2 with remaining games against Purdue, Illinois, and Nebraska, Iowa's destiny is out in front of them to make their first appearance in the playoff under head coach Kirk Ferentz in his 28th season. The offense isn't anything to call home about but the defense continues to be one of the nation's best units under the widely considered best defensive coordinator in the country in Phil Parker.

When Ryan Browne has been given time to throw the ball this season, he has done a pretty good job of finding his playmakers at receiver. The improvement of those receivers from last year has allowed Browne to take a big leap in his development but that quickly goes away when he isn't given a clean pocket to work with. That starts up front with the offensive line that features some very promising but young players like Rico Schreiber, Brock Brownfield, Nuku Mafi, and Marques Easley.

Iowa's defensive front relies heavily on pressure from their front four led by players like Joseph Anderson (4 sacks), Bryce Hawthorne (3.5 sacks/8TFL's), Drew Campbell (2.5 sacks/4TFL's), and several other players. DC Phill Parker's main priority is to ensure explosive plays are limited and force offenses into long, sustained drives that end in mistakes. It's a formula that is very simple but incredibly effective for the Hawkeyes as they consistently rank near the top of the B1G every season in total defense.

What is most effective about this scheme is that the Hawkeyes force QB's into mistakes and they have been able to get turnovers at a high rate. This season has been on the lower side of forcing turnovers with just 9 but the fundamental aspects of the defense remain: don't miss tackles, limit big plays, force offenses to sustained drives, and don't put yourself in bad situations by blitzing too much (roughly 20% of the time).

In Iowa's recent victory over Northwestern, running back LJ Phillips racked up 128 rushing yards on 21 carries to keep control of the tempo. Purdue's defense, which has struggled to play in the backfield most of the season, must hold Iowa to minimum yards on first down to force QB Hank Brown into drop back passing situations. One aspect that has seemingly gotten better over the last several weeks on the defensive side of the ball is that they are generating some turnovers. That has got to continue by forcing Iowa into obvious passing downs where the defensive backs can worry solely about defending the pass.

Through nine games, Purdue has struggled to consistently disrupt plays in the backfield, surrendering 170.8 rushing yards per game at a 5.2-yard clip while ranking 86th nationally in stuff rate. Purdue doesn't need to suddenly become a dominant TFL team, rather, they simply need to win enough early-down reps to hold Phillips and the Hawkeye ground game to two or three yards on first down.

Doing so forces quarterback Hank Brown out of his play-action comfort zone and into pure dropback situations. While Brown has been efficient managing games this season (1,316 yards, nine touchdowns, four interceptions), Iowa isn't built to win shootouts when forced into 3rd-and-long. More importantly, winning first down unlocks what has quietly become Purdue's biggest defensive bright spot over the last month: takeaways. After recording just two turnovers through the end of September, the Boilermakers have rattled off nine more in the weeks since. When Purdue's defensive backs don't have to worry about run support or biting on play-action fakes, they can sit on routes, play aggressive coverage, and generate the kind of game-flipping turnovers required to steal a win at Kinnick.

Against Maryland, Purdue left the door wide open in the first half by settling for field goals instead of getting into the endzone. Yes, Purdue has one of the best kickers in the country with Jacobo Echeverria Lozano but Purdue really should have been leading by double digits. Instead, Purdue led just 12-7 instead of potentially 24-7 and that would have meant a very different second half.

Purdue does have the 19th rated red zone offense on the season, largely because of their freshman kicker connecting on 21-22 kicks this season. That is good for 2nd in the country and he likely has an argument for All American Honors alongside All B1G recognition. However, the Boilers have got to convert their opportunities into touchdowns if they want to beat the Hawkeyes on the road.

Iowa, at home, is too good of a football team for Purdue to settle for field goals when scoring opportunities are presented to them. Notably, Ryan Browne has got to make high level throws when the field shrinks and the throwing windows get tighter and tighter. If that isn't going to happen, Purdue better hope their offensive line is able to open up running lanes for Fame Ijeboi.

#2740. Rams place WR Puka Nacua on IR with knee, turf toe injuries

The Los Angeles Rams placed Puka Nacua on injured reserve, the team announced Thursday. The move will sideline the receiver for at least four games after he suffered multiple injuries Sunday.

In a connected move, the Rams have signed receiver Brennan Presley to the active roster from the practice squad, and signed WR Tyler Scott to the practice squad.

Nacua sustained injuries late in the Rams' win over the Washington Commanders on Sunday. He was later diagnosed with MCL and PCL sprains in his right knee and a turf toe injury.

Head coach Sean McVay told reporters Wednesday that Nacua will miss "a significant period of time." McVay initially said the receiver would not go on IR due to "some semantics with the roster," but that appears to have changed.

By being on IR, the earliest Nacua can return is against the Dallas Cowboys on Dec. 20.

Nacua, who missed two games early in the season with a hip injury, has had a strong 2026 season. In seven games, he has 70 receptions for 715 yards and four touchdowns. The Commanders' game was his most productive of the season before the injuries, as Nacua picked up 14 catches for 150 yards and a touchdown.

Nacua joins Davante Adams on IR; Adams has been there since Week 6 with a ruptured hamstring. McVay said Wednesday he is hoping for Adams to return in Week 13, meaning it will still be a couple of weeks of playing with a shrunken receiver core.

#2739. Miami's Chuck Martin slams Speedos in videoboard upright penalty rant

Miami RedHawks head coach Chuck Martin had a bizarre, lengthy and memorable reaction to the team's penalty for showing multiple uprights on the videoboard during a Mid-American Conference football win Nov. 10 against Ohio at Oxford's Yager Stadium.

With the Bobcats leading 17-7, Ohio kicker Brack Peacock attempted a field goal that hit the right upright and missed. Miami was penalized for unsportsmanlike conduct for showing multiple uprights on the videoboard behind the uprights themselves.

"On the previous play, there were depictions of the field-goal uprights on the scoreboard," the official announced just before halftime. "That is a foul for unsportsmanlike conduct against Miami. Half the distance to the goal, automatic first down."

"It was so weird, because he missed the kick," Martin told reporters Nov. 12. "There was no flag. We huddled up. We sent our offense out. There's two seconds left. We were going to take a knee, obviously. There's two seconds left. Our guys are on the field. The ball's there. There's still no flag. Now we're two minutes past the play. And there's a group of officials standing there, and I didn't think nothing of it. There's nothing going on. We're just waiting for them to put the ball in play. And the next thing I know, I see the guy just drop a flag, like literally standing there talking, and then he just puts a flag on the ground."

"I was like, what's going on?" Martin continued. "And at that point, I just thought somebody said something. One of the players on the two teams was complaining about something. Got an unsportsmanlike (flag). That's what I just figured, like, where else? And then a guy comes up to me on the sidelines, and again, it was, their job is to de-escalate the situation. Good officials de-escalate everything. Bad officials escalate everything. Doesn't matter what sport it is."

"In my wildest dream, did I think we'd be getting an unsportsmanlike conduct on something we put on a videoboard?" Martin asked. "One, I didn't even know that was possible. I know there's a rule that said, like, you can't play music on third down. ... I've seen the pictures now, because I didn't even know what was on the scoreboard. Like, they had goal posts on the scoreboard."

"I was like, 'So what?'" Martin added. "They had goal posts on the scoreboard. They had Casper the Friendly Ghost on the scoreboard. Who cared? Like, who cares what they put on the videoboard? Like, if I kicked, like, there's zero percent chance that's a distraction. Like, zero percent. I kicked. I kicked in high school and I kicked in college. I know a lot of kickers. Like, there's zero percent chance that's a distraction. Zero percent. And then I saw the picture from behind. ... Like, was he confused which goal posts they, I mean, it was, I mean, the picture from behind is ridiculous."

"Like, there's no confusion there," Martin said. "There's zero confusion. I mean, it's ridiculous. And then you put your, you take your steps, you put your head down, and then you roll. Like, it's not like you're looking at the goal posts when you're kicking, okay? Now I'm shooting a free throw, right? And there's a glass backboard that you can see through, right? And that's really where my line of sight is. Like, I can see, and there's all these students, and there's grown men, you know, college-age grown men in Speedos with shower caps on, jumping up and down in front of me, you know, in little Speedos. Like, they're not big Speedos. Like, they're really tiny Speedos. Like, when I'm not shooting free throws at basketball games or if I'm watching games on TV, it's really uncomfortable."

"It's uncomfortable that someone would come to a game and do that," Martin said. "I really appreciate it because we're trying to throw off the other team. Like, so I don't even, like, but that's not a distraction."

"There's no, underneath, like, it looks like stick figures (on the videoboard)," Martin joked. "Like, somebody looks like your fourth grader was drawing stick figures. Like, whoever came up with the graphic, isn't, like, isn't, like, on the cutting edge of, like, you know, if we were trying to distract them, we could be a little better. So, but again, it's just par for the course. It is what it is. And I don't, not anything like any, like, you saw my reaction. I was like, okay, we got to play the next play. You know, got to play the next play."

RedHawks basketball coach Travis Steele told ESPN college hoops analysts before the MAC tournament that he planned to wear a Speedo at the watch party in March. He changed his mind.

"I've gotten a bunch of (Speedos) sent to me in the mail, believe it or not," Steele had said. "I gotta see which one fits and which one's gonna flatter me the most. Listen, when Rece (Davis) put me on 'GameDay' and put me on the spot, I said, 'Listen, that's a heckuva problem to have if I have to wear a Speedo.' So I've gotta get some extra workouts and watch my diets here over the next week."

#2738. NFL Injury Report, Week 10: Latest news, updates for Puka Nacua, George Pickens, more players for fantasy football

It's the halfway point of the 2026 NFL season and by now you likely have weathered plenty of injuries on your fantasy football rosters. We have a handful of big names we're tracking going into Week 10 while four teams are on bye — the Bears, Broncos, Buccaneers and Eagles. Below we'll update you on the latest injury news, plus provide some useful fantasy football analysis.

Sam Darnold, SEA (quad/ribs) — Out for Week 10

Drew Lock, SEA (oblique) — Should be good to start

Deshaun Watson, CLE (concussion) — Set to start

Gardner Minshew, ARI (elbow) — On IR with torn UCL

Mahomes: At the time of Mahomes' injury in Week 9, it looked as though we were watching a QB who may be done for the season. But after exiting due to an elbow injury, Mahomes was able to return in the Chiefs' 35-12 win over the Jets on Sunday. Mahomes completed 23-of-31 passes for 242 yards and two scores, posting fewer than 20 fantasy points for the fifth time in the past six games.

Kenneth Walker III continues to be the focal point of the offense as the passing game lacks depth and a vertical threat. The Chiefs face the Falcons in Week 10 and Mahomes was a full practice participant Wednesday, a good sign for him being able to play. If he's able to go, it'll be a chance for him to work with new receiver Josh Downs, who came over in a trade with the Colts on Tuesday.

Seahawks QBs: Head coach Mike Macdonald already went on the radio Monday and said Darnold will be out Week 10 against the Raiders. Lock underwent tests on an oblique injury he suffered Sunday and those came back "good," so he's in line to start again. The Raiders have been a great fantasy matchup for QBs this season, allowing the fifth-most points to the position. However, the Seattle offense has struggled a bit with lack of depth behind Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Lock is back in the QB2 streaming convo for Sunday and isn't a bad spot start if you have Caleb Williams or Bo Nix on bye.

Minshew: The Cardinals QB is on IR with a torn UCL. That means rookie Carson Beck will start. If you remember back to the preseason, Beck was actually pretty good. There's a chance this is a good move overall for the offense, particularly TE Trey McBride. But Arizona is down WR Michael Wilson (neck) and Beck won't have many other options in the passing game. In Superflex, Beck is worth a speculative add to see how he does in Week 10 against the Rams.

Willis: The Dolphins surprised us before the trade deadline by placing Willis on IR, which could mean he's done for the season this late in the year. He'll miss at least the next four games, which would mean the soonest he could be back is Week 14 against Chicago. 2025 sixth-round pick Kyle McCord is the backup and will start in Week 10 versus the Colts. Brady Cook will be the backup.

Miami's passing offense enters Week 10 ranked 30th in the NFL. Chances are it doesn't get much better with McCord under center, but we'll need to see. It's a downgrade to receivers like Malik Washington, Greg Dulcich and Caleb Douglas in the short term until we assess things. Ollie Gordon II could be leaned on a bit more, and McCord may use the RB and Dulcich as safety valves.

TreVeyon Henderson, NE (illness — ruled out)

Josh Jacobs, GB (finger) — Report: Out a max of three weeks

Travis Etienne Jr., NO (hamstring) — Chance to return this week

Bhayshul Tuten, JAX (ankle/foot) — DNP on Wednesday

Etienne: This is one to watch going into the weekend. Etienne got in a limited practice on Thursday and will likely hold a questionable tag going into Sunday's game versus the Panthers. If Etienne is active, he could be on some sort of pitch count. But he could still leech some touches away from Audric Estime, who was a trending waiver-wire add this week. Alvin Kamara also got nine touches last week against the Browns. Estime likely leads the backfield with Etienne out. But if the veteran returns, it could water down the touches between the three backs.

Patriots RBs: Stevenson exited Sunday's blowout loss to the Packers early and did not return. Henderson has missed the past two games after being hospitalized due to "unexplained neurological symptoms." Stevenson missed practice Wednesday and was limited on Thursday, but will reportedly be sidelined multiple weeks.

The Patriots face the Lions in Germany this week, which means Corey Kiner is likely to take over as the lead back. He finished with a solid 8-55-1 rushing line against Green Bay, though most of that production was on a fourth-quarter drive when the game was essentially over. Lan Larison would be the RB2 for New England. Keep an eye on this as Stevenson getting back on the practice field Thursday is telling. Maybe there's a shot he's active. But if he's out, Kiner is a decent RB3/flex play.

Jacobs: On the other side of that game, Jacobs suffered a fractured finger in the win over the Patriots and didn't return. Rushing duties were then split between Pierre Strong Jr. and Kaleb Johnson with MarShawn Lloyd out. Johnson rushed for 68 yards on 14 carries with a score. He looked pretty good running the ball for a team that has struggled to do so all season. But it was also in a blowout. Even so, Johnson is a proactive add off the waiver wire with Jacobs expected to miss time. Green Bay faces the Vikings in Week 10 before the bye and it would be hard to trust any Packers RB against one of the best defenses in the NFL. Johnson will be a risky flex play against Minnesota in Week 10. Strong isn't a bad add in deeper PPR formats and keep an eye on Lloyd, who could be back soon.

Puka Nacua, LAR (knee/turf toe) — Placed on IR

Michael Wilson, ARI (neck) — Out for season

Luther Burden III, CHI (concussion) — on bye

Nacua: The wideout was placed on injured reserve Thursday, meaning he will miss at least the next four games with knee sprains and turf toe. The Rams are already without Davante Adams, but McVay did offer hope that the veteran WR could return from a ruptured hamstring as soon as Week 13. For now, there isn't much WR depth. Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell and the trio of tight ends — Tyler Higbee, Colby Parkinson and Davis Allen — will need to step up. We'd throw Terrance Ferguson into that group, but he remains on IR and isn't expected back in Week 10. L.A. should lean more on its run game with Kyren Williams and Blake Corum.

With Nacua out, it's a downgrade to the passing game and Matthew Stafford's fantasy outlook. It's a slight bump up for Williams and Corum, both of whom see plenty of work in the passing game plenty. The Rams take on the Cardinals before their bye in Week 11, which is an easy draw for the run game. Mumpfield isn't a bad waiver-wire add, along with Atwell in deeper formats. But don't expect any receiver to get the type of volume Nacua did.

Michael Wilson: The WR will miss the rest of the season due to a neck injury. It's a tough blow for managers who were hoping for more following the Marvin Harrison Jr. trade. Instead, Wilson struggled, failing to reach double-digit fantasy points in four of the past five games. With Jalen Brooks and Kendrick Bourne on injured reserve, Arizona is very, very thin at WR.

Simi Fehoko, Reggie Virgil and Devin Duvernay all played significant snaps in Week 9 against Seattle. None of them did much, while Trey McBride was obviously the main target for Gardner Minshew. Though, Minshew is on IR with a torn UCL and the team will start rookie Carson Beck at QB this week.

As a result, CeeDee Lamb went off for 10-195-1 while third-string WR Ryan Flournoy was quiet with two catches for 53 yards. Dallas leaned on the run game, leading most of the first half. If Pickens is out again, Flournoy remains a flex option, while Lamb would remain a target hog and elite WR1.

#2737. Miami's Chuck Martin slams Speedos in videoboard upright penalty rant

Miami RedHawks head coach Chuck Martin had a bizarre, lengthy and memorable reaction to the team's penalty for showing multiple uprights on the videoboard during a Mid-American Conference football win Nov. 10 against Ohio at Oxford's Yager Stadium.

With the Bobcats leading 17-7, Ohio kicker Brack Peacock attempted a field goal that hit the right upright and missed. Miami was penalized for unsportsmanlike conduct for showing multiple uprights on the videoboard behind the uprights themselves.

"On the previous play, there were depictions of the field-goal uprights on the scoreboard," the official announced just before halftime. "That is a foul for unsportsmanlike conduct against Miami. Half the distance to the goal, automatic first down."

"It was so weird, because he missed the kick," Martin told reporters Nov. 12. "There was no flag. We huddled up. We sent our offense out. There's two seconds left. We were going to take a knee, obviously. There's two seconds left. Our guys are on the field. The ball's there. There's still no flag. Now we're two minutes past the play. And there's a group of officials standing there, and I didn't think nothing of it. There's nothing going on. We're just waiting for them to put the ball in play. And the next thing I know, I see the guy just drop a flag, like literally standing there talking, and then he just puts a flag on the ground."

"I was like, what's going on?" Martin continued. "And at that point, I just thought somebody said something. One of the players on the two teams was complaining about something. Got an unsportsmanlike (flag). That's what I just figured, like, where else? And then a guy comes up to me on the sidelines, and again, it was, their job is to de-escalate the situation. Good officials de-escalate everything. Bad officials escalate everything. Doesn't matter what sport it is."

"In my wildest dream, did I think we'd be getting an unsportsmanlike conduct on something we put on a videoboard?" Martin asked. "One, I didn't even know that was possible. I know there's a rule that said, like, you can't play music on third down. ... I've seen the pictures now, because I didn't even know what was on the scoreboard. Like, they had goal posts on the scoreboard."

"I was like, 'So what?'" Martin added. "They had goal posts on the scoreboard. They had Casper the Friendly Ghost on the scoreboard. Who cared? Like, who cares what they put on the videoboard? Like, if I kicked, like, there's zero percent chance that's a distraction. Like, zero percent. I kicked. I kicked in high school and I kicked in college. I know a lot of kickers. Like, there's zero percent chance that's a distraction. Zero percent. And then I saw the picture from behind. ... Like, was he confused which goal posts they, I mean, it was, I mean, the picture from behind is ridiculous."

"Like, there's no confusion there," Martin said. "There's zero confusion. I mean, it's ridiculous. And then you put your, you take your steps, you put your head down, and then you roll. Like, it's not like you're looking at the goal posts when you're kicking, okay? Now I'm shooting a free throw, right? And there's a glass backboard that you can see through, right? And that's really where my line of sight is. Like, I can see, and there's all these students, and there's grown men, you know, college-age grown men in Speedos with shower caps on, jumping up and down in front of me, you know, in little Speedos. Like, they're not big Speedos. Like, they're really tiny Speedos. Like, when I'm not shooting free throws at basketball games or if I'm watching games on TV, it's really uncomfortable."

"It's uncomfortable that someone would come to a game and do that," Martin said. "I really appreciate it because we're trying to throw off the other team. Like, so I don't even, like, but that's not a distraction."

"There's no, underneath, like, it looks like stick figures (on the videoboard)," Martin joked. "Like, somebody looks like your fourth grader was drawing stick figures. Like, whoever came up with the graphic, isn't, like, isn't, like, on the cutting edge of, like, you know, if we were trying to distract them, we could be a little better. So, but again, it's just par for the course. It is what it is. And I don't, not anything like any, like, you saw my reaction. I was like, okay, we got to play the next play. You know, got to play the next play."

RedHawks basketball coach Travis Steele told ESPN college hoops analysts before the MAC tournament that he planned to wear a Speedo at the watch party in March. He changed his mind.

"I've gotten a bunch of (Speedos) sent to me in the mail, believe it or not," Steele had said. "I gotta see which one fits and which one's gonna flatter me the most. Listen, when Rece (Davis) put me on 'GameDay' and put me on the spot, I said, 'Listen, that's a heckuva problem to have if I have to wear a Speedo.' So I've gotta get some extra workouts and watch my diets here over the next week."

#2736. Rams place Puka Nacua on IR after all. Where does LA go from here?

Puka Nacua is head to injured reserve after all.

The Los Angeles Rams officially placed their star wide receiver on IR on Thursday, Nov. 12, a day after head coach Sean McVay told reporters that Nacua would miss significant time but avoid IR due to "roster semantics." Per NFL rules, a team can designate up to eight players for return from injured reserve in a single season.

The Rams, plagued by injuries all year, have already designated three players – Myles Garrett, rookie tackle Keagen Trost and running back Ronnie Rivers – and a fourth, Terrance Ferguson, is expected back in a couple weeks after tweaking his hamstring in practice last Friday. Kobie Turner and Davante Adams figure to be the fifth and sixth players to return for IR, with Nacua presumably being the seventh in at least four weeks from now.

Nacua injured his PCL and MCL during a jet sweep on the final offensive play in their Week 9 win over the Washington Commanders, in which he put up 150 yards and a touchdown on 14 receptions. WR Brennan Presley was signed from the practice squad and the Rams signed Tyler Scott to the practice squad in corresponding moves. Xavier Smith was signed from the San Francisco 49ers' practice squad on Tuesday after Jordan Whittington was placed on IR with a back injury.

Assuming Nacua returns in the earliest window possible, Week 14 against the 49ers, that means the Rams would only be able to bring back one of Whittington, offensive lineman Justin Dedich, running back Dean Connors and lineman Steve Avila (who has not been officially placed on IR yet) barring any other major injuries.

McVay told reporters on Wednesday that the team hopes Adams can return after Week 12 vs. the Green Bay Packers, a welcome bit of good news for a receiver room that has been decimated in the last few weeks.

"Guys will be asked to step up," McVay told reporters on Monday ahead of the trade deadline. "Puka has always had a pretty large target share based on his production and the different things that he does and because of the way that you're able to get him the football because of some of the unselfish stuff he does in the run game.

"... There are other guys that are very capable of doing some good stuff for us. We'll look to see those guys step up and it'll be great opportunity for them in spite of it being a bummer for those guys that are out."

#2735. Eintracht's Kalimuendo pursuit could push Tottenham- and Juventus-linked Ebnoutalib towards January exit

Younes Ebnoutalib has been in impressive form in front of goal this season, scoring eight goals in 11 appearances for Eintracht Frankfurt so far. Despite this, the 23-year-old forward has not always been a regular starter.

Eintracht coach Adi Hütter currently favours a 4-2-3-1 formation, meaning either Ebnoutalib or Jonathan Burkardt has had to settle for a place on the bench from time to time.

At the same time, reports suggest that Eintracht Frankfurt are looking to further strengthen their attacking options in January by making another attempt to sign Nottingham Forest's Arnaud Kalimuendo, who scored six goals during a loan spell at the club in the second half of last season.

Should the Frenchman return, Ebnoutalib could fear slipping to third choice up front, potentially limiting his playing time even more and making it more difficult for him to retain his place in Jürgen Klopp's Germany squad.

Although Sport Bild reports that Eintracht are keen to extend Ebnoutalib's contract, the German publication speculates that a move for Kalimuendo could push the striker towards a January exit.

The 23-year-old has been linked with several clubs, including Juventus and Tottenham Hotspur. However, a move abroad doesn't currently appear to be an option, as Ebnoutalib would prefer to remain in the Bundesliga, according to the report.

#2734. Sports Media Loves Second Chances Until Dianna Russini Needs One

Apparently, Dianna Russini didn't apologize enough. Didn't explain enough and didn't show enough remorse to satisfy the sports media's newly appointed Department of Moral Superiority. So, now what?

Do we revoke her press credentials for life? Force her to stand before 300 sportswriters and beg for forgiveness before reporting a rumored trade? The reaction to Russini's return has been something to behold.

After seven months away, she returned with a new show and column for BetUS. Russini discussing her family, the difficult months away and her excitement about covering football again. What she didn't do was directly address the controversy involving Patriots coach Mike Vrabel.

The media wanted answers, accountability and perhaps a televised confession followed by a walk of shame through the NFL owners' meetings. Who appointed us judge, jury and executioner?

Let's establish something immediately. Dianna Russini crossed a serious line. The Athletic investigated her relationship with Vrabel after photographs surfaced of them together at an Arizona resort. Its review concluded that the relationship violated company standards and should have been disclosed to editors. Regardless of whether it was romantic or not.

Journalism depends on trust. If editors can't trust you to disclose potential conflicts, why should audiences trust your reporting?

Here's where the story gets interesting. The Athletic reviewed hundreds of articles, videos and podcast appearances. It found no inaccuracies in Russini's work involving Vrabel, although it criticized some coverage as overly flattering and recommended editors' notes. That's an important distinction. Violating professional standards doesn't automatically mean every story you've reported was dishonest. Also, it certainly doesn't mean you should never work again.

Now, let's discuss something our industry conveniently avoids. The NFL insider business is all about relationships. Not just professional handshakes and exchanging Christmas cards. We're talking about reporters spending years developing close relationships with players, coaches, agents and front-office executives.

They text at midnight, share meals, protect sources and sometimes become friends with the very people they're supposed to cover objectively.

It's an uncomfortable dance. Insiders need information, while sources want favorable access, influence or simply someone willing to tell their side. Everybody wants something. The closer those relationships become, the harder it can be to distinguish independent reporting from delivering somebody else's message.

Let's not pretend Russini invented this problem.

Plenty of reporters are awfully cozy with the people they cover. Some practically have reserved parking spaces outside NFL general managers' offices. Others deliver information so favorable to a particular organization that you wonder whether the press release came with a byline.

Does that make every insider unethical? Of course not. Relationships are how this business works, but they're also where its biggest ethical dangers begin. Russini took it too far. The larger issue isn't whether reporters develop relationships. It's whether they maintain enough professional distance to tell the truth when those relationships become inconvenient.

That's the standard everyone should face, including the people currently throwing stones.

Sports media is filled with enormous egos, questionable conflicts and people who've received second, third and occasionally fourth chances. Some of these glass houses have floor-to-ceiling windows, and the people inside are throwing bricks.

There's another uncomfortable reality here.

Women in sports media have spent decades fighting unfair assumptions about how they obtain access and information. Russini's decisions gave people who already embrace those stereotypes another excuse to question women doing outstanding work. She should be held accountable because she's a journalist, not because she's a woman. However, she should also recognize that her decisions affected more than her own reputation.

Now, can we remember who matters in this business? The fans. Remember them? The people who watch, listen, read and ultimately determine whether any of us has a job?

Here's a bold prediction. If Russini breaks a blockbuster NFL story tomorrow, fans will read it. If she reports that a franchise quarterback is being traded, nobody's refusing to click because her apology didn't satisfy the sports media ethics committee. They're going to want to know who's getting traded and whether their team gave up three first-round picks to acquire him.

Fans want information, accuracy, access and news before everybody else has it. That's the business. Credibility matters enormously. If Russini starts getting stories wrong, demonstrates favoritism or becomes nothing more than a mouthpiece for sources, she has a serious problem.

If she consistently delivers accurate, independent reporting, shouldn't that count?

I'm also curious about her new home. BetUS is an offshore sportsbook, and the relationship between gambling companies and journalists deserves scrutiny. Information moves betting markets, making editorial independence and transparency especially important. Russini should expect more scrutiny than most reporters because of what happened.

She earned that, but scrutiny isn't the same as rooting for failure.

We celebrate redemption stories in sports constantly. Players screw up, coaches screw up and executives screw up. Yet we preach accountability, growth and second chances. Then someone in our industry makes a mistake, and suddenly everybody's auditioning for district attorney.

Besides, would another apology really satisfy the critics? A prepared statement would be called scripted. Tears would be dismissed as playing the victim. A detailed explanation would generate demands for even more details. There's no satisfying a jury that's already reached its verdict.

Russini lost a prominent job. Her reputation took a beating, and her personal life became national entertainment. Those are real consequences. She owes future employers honesty, audiences transparency and accurate reporting. But also herself a better understanding of professional boundaries.

What she doesn't owe is a lifetime of apologies to every sports media personality with a podcast microphone.

Maybe she'll rebuild her credibility, and maybe she won't. That depends on what she reports, how she reports it and whether people believe her. We're not here to decide who gets into heaven; we're here to inform and entertain an audience.

Dianna Russini doesn't need the sports media's forgiveness. She needs the fans' trust. If she earns it back, the audience will decide her future, not the people throwing stones from inside their own glass houses.

#2732. Without Steph Curry, Warriors rookie is going to be put to ultimate test

Yaxel Lendeborg has never lacked confidence.

When the Warriors were in the running to acquire LeBron James, the rookie expressed excitement about potentially playing alongside one of the greatest players of all time but also told the California Post, "Hopefully he doesn't take away my minutes."

And after Lendeborg and Luka Doncic exchanged trash talk when the Lakers played the Warriors in their season opener, Lendeborg said he "lost all respect" for one of the NBA's biggest superstars, calling out his "whining" and "complaining."

After Steph Curry suffered an oblique abdominal tear in the Warriors' 115-108 loss to the Rockets on Wednesday, Lendeborg is now the team's star.

Curry will be reevaluated in two weeks and is expected to be sidelined close to a month, according to ESPN, meaning it's now up to the 24-year-old to carry the franchise.

And so far he has walked the walk, averaging 21.7 points, 7.4 rebounds and 3.7 assists while surging to the top of the Rookie of the Year race.

That's a different challenge altogether. We're really about to see what Lendeborg is capable of, especially considering Curry had opened the season playing out of his mind.

The 38-year-old Curry was having an MVP-caliber campaign, entering Wednesday's game averaging 30.6 points, 4.3 assists and 4.1 rebounds for the Warriors, who had stunned the league by winning eight straight games.

Golden State Warriors player Steph Curry attends the season opener against the Los Angeles Lakers in Los Angeles on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. London Entertainment

Overnight, Lendeborg has gone from being a sidekick to the main character.

Draymond Green said he already saw glimmers of that happening Wednesday.

"It's funny because the thing that he's going to have to learn and understand is, all right, Steph wasn't out there, KD (Kevin Durant) was off the court, you look around, you're probably the best player on the floor," Green told reporters. "Regardless of team.

"I think there was a point he realized, ding, ding, ding, and he started attacking, and the game flipped for us. I think that's something that he's going to have to realize really fast. There will be oftentimes where he can possibly be the best player on the floor regardless of the team. We need him to show that. He doesn't have a problem doing it."

Lendeborg has been one of the season's biggest stories.

Golden State Warriors player Yaxel Lendeborg, left, and head coach Steve Kerr smile during a game against the Houston Rockets on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

The Warriors' 11th pick in the draft breathed new life into Curry's career during what was thought to be a lost season after Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody suffered injuries that would sideline them for the first few months and Kristaps Porzingis announced he was stepping away from basketball indefinitely.

Lendeborg picked up the slack. Brandin Podziemski is making major contributions, averaging career highs in points (17.3), field-goal percentage (48.1) and 3-point shooting (39.7%). And Green is capable of bottling up anyone in the league on any given night.

The person who's going to feel that most is Lendeborg, who's going to experience a different type of defensive pressure than he's ever seen.

Curry is a four-time MVP. He carried the Warriors to four championships in eight years from 2015-2022 before the dynasty began flailing, failing to advance past the second round of the playoffs the last four years.

Lendeborg helped resuscitate Golden State. Now he's going to have to put it on his shoulders.

Lendeborg wants that. He wants to be a star. But can he handle it now?

Golden State Warriors forward Yaxel Lendeborg (1) shoots against Houston Rockets forward Kevin Durant (7) in Houston, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. AP Photo/Ashley Landis

Green made waves at the top of the season for saying the Warriors found the "next face of the franchise" in Lendeborg. That meant a lot coming from Green, who doesn't give that type of praise easily, especially to a rookie.

We're going to get a preview of whether he was right. Whether Lendeborg is ready. Whether he's able to handle the pressure.

Last season, the Warriors went 13-26 without Curry, who missed 27 straight games because of runner's knee.

They're better equipped to deal with Curry's absence this time around because of an outspoken and talented rookie who's about to be thrust into a situation he was supposed to be eased into.

For however long Curry is out, Lendeborg is the face of the Warriors.

His confidence is going to be put to the ultimate test.
